what_a: Returns a copy of the given string with all lowercase ASCII letters converted to uppercase, leaving other characters unchanged.
what_b: Returns a copy of the given string with all uppercase ASCII letters converted to lowercase, leaving other characters unchanged.
diff: A converts 'a'-'z' to uppercase and leaves all other characters unchanged, while B converts 'A'-'Z' to lowercase and leaves all other characters unchanged. They differ for every input containing a letter, e.g. upperCase("abc") yields "ABC" but lowered("abc") yields "abc". Both return the input unchanged when it has no letters of the relevant case.

what_a: Splits a string into a list of non-empty words, treating spaces and tabs as separators.
what_b: Splits a string into a list of non-empty words, treating spaces and tabs as separators.
diff: Only for inputs with text.size() >= 2^32 bytes. There, B's `u32 i` wraps to 0 and the loop never ends, while A terminates correctly. All other inputs produce identical output.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Converts a 32-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives and "0" for zero.
diff: For every i32-representable value the outputs match (e.g. 0, 7, -42, INT32_MIN gives "-2147483648"). They differ for i64 values outside the i32 range: bufferInt(4294967296) returns "4294967296", but gearNum needs the argument narrowed to i32, which truncates it (to 0 here). bufferInt(INT64_MIN) is also undefined behaviour because `-v` overflows, while gearNum never negates an overflowing value.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal text string, handling zero and negative values, with no game meaning.
what_b: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, handling negative values and zero without any game meaning.
diff: Only for v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). Function B returns "-9223372036854775808". Function A negates it, which overflows (undefined behaviour), so the value stays negative and the recursion never terminates, ending in a stack overflow. All other inputs give identical strings.

what_a: Looks up an item's definition record from the game's item table by its id, returning a pointer to it or null when the id is negative or out of range.
what_b: Looks up an item definition by its numeric id, returning a pointer into the item table or null when the id is zero, negative, or out of range.
diff: For `id == 0` with a nonempty `items` array, A returns `&ctx.data.items[0]` while B returns `nullptr`. Negative and out-of-range ids return `nullptr` in both. A takes an `Item` and reads `item.id`, while B takes the raw `i32`, which is an argument-form change only.

what_a: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by converting the signed index to an unsigned value and indexing the party's member array, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by casting the signed index to unsigned and indexing the party's members array, with no game rule applied.
diff: For the same non-const Party argument, both return the same element. Function A accepts only non-const Party and returns a mutable Character&, so it is the only one usable where the result is modified or the party is non-const. Function B accepts const Party and returns const Character&, so it is the only one usable with a const Party, and it cannot be used to modify the element. Both perform the same unchecked i32-to-u32 cast, so negative or out-of-range indices behave identically (undefined behaviour from out-of-bounds access).

what_a: Joins the words of a string vector from index `from` onward into a single space-separated string.
what_b: Joins the words of a string vector from a given starting index into one space-separated string.
diff: They differ only when the joined range starts with one or more empty strings. For example, with w = ["", "a"] and from = 0, A returns " a" (leading space) and B returns "a". Likewise w = ["", "", "x"] gives " " + " x" = "  x" in A versus "x" in B. Every other input, including empty strings after the first non-empty element and from >= w.size() (both return ""), gives identical results.

what_a: Joins the words of a string vector from index `from` onward into a single space-separated string.
what_b: Joins the words of a string vector from index `from` up to `to` (clamped to the vector's size) into a single space-separated string.
diff: They differ whenever an empty string appears before the first non-empty output. A puts a separator before every element after `from`, while B only adds one when `out` is non-empty. Examples: `{"", "b"}` from 0 gives `" b"` in A and `"b"` in B. `{"", ""}` from 0 gives `" "` in A and `""` in B. `{"", "", "x"}` from 0 gives `"  x"` in A and `"x"` in B. Also, B's `to` bound truncates the range (`{"a","b","c"}`, from 0, to 2 gives `"a b"` in B and `"a b c"` in A), and A has no equivalent parameter, so B can be replaced by A only at call sites where `to >= w.size()`. Otherwise results match, including `from >= w.size()` (both return `""`) and inputs with no leading empty strings.

what_a: Joins the words of a string vector from a given starting index into one space-separated string.
what_b: Joins the words of a string vector from index `from` up to `to` (clamped to the vector's size) into a single space-separated string.
diff: They differ whenever `to < w.size()`. Function A always joins through the end of `w`, while B stops before index `to`. For example, with `w = {"a","b","c"}` and `from = 0`, A returns `"a b c"` but B with `to = 2` returns `"a b"`. With `to >= w.size()`, or with `from >= w.size()`, the two return identical results. Both also share the same quirk where an empty element suppresses the separator before the next element.

what_a: Returns a copy of the given string with all lowercase ASCII letters converted to uppercase, leaving other characters unchanged.
what_b: Returns a copy of the input string with all ASCII uppercase letters converted to lowercase.
diff: Function A maps 'a'-'z' to 'A'-'Z' and Function B maps 'A'-'Z' to 'a'-'z', so they disagree on every ASCII letter (e.g. "abc" gives "ABC" from A but "abc" from B; "ABC" gives "ABC" from A but "abc" from B). They agree only on strings with no ASCII letters, such as "123 !?", and on the empty string.

what_a: Returns a copy of the input string with all ASCII uppercase letters converted to lowercase.
what_b: Returns a copy of the given string with all uppercase ASCII letters converted to lowercase, leaving other characters unchanged.
diff: Only for strings of 2^32 bytes (4,294,967,296) or longer. There, B's `u32 i` wraps around before reaching `r.size()`, so B loops forever while A returns the lowercased copy. For every shorter input, including embedded NULs, empty strings, and non-ASCII bytes, both produce identical results.

what_a: Linear search over the game's floor list that returns a pointer to the floor whose dungeon level matches the given level, or null if none does.
what_b: Linear search over the loaded floor definitions that returns a pointer to the floor whose levelNum matches the given dungeon level, or null if none does.
diff: Every input differs in kind, not just value. A searches `s.game.floors` (per-session mutable `FloorState`, matched on `dungeonLevel`) and returns a mutable `FloorState*`. B searches `data.floors` (static `GameData`, matched on `levelNum`) and returns a `const FloorDef*`. For the same level number, A yields the runtime state of that floor and B yields its static definition, so they cannot substitute for each other.

what_a: Reads an integer field `k` from a JSON object `o`, returning it as an i32 or 0 if the key is missing.
what_b: Reads a boolean field by key from a JSON object, returning false if the key is missing.
diff: They return different types and convert different JSON values. For a missing key both return a default (geti gives 0, getb gives false). For a present key with an integer value, geti returns that integer, while getb calls asBool on a number, which may not give a meaningful result. For a present key with a boolean value, getb returns it, while geti calls asInt on a bool, whose result depends on JsonValue::asInt, which I did not inspect.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 or 2 ASCII digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if the text is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a 1-based party member number, returning 0 if the input is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
diff: Both accept only 1-2 digit strings and parse them the same way, but they report results differently. A returns bool and writes `out` only on success, so "0" and "00" give true with out=0 and any failure (non-digit, empty, too long) gives false with `out` untouched. B returns the value directly and uses 0 as its failure sentinel, so "0" and "00" return 0, indistinguishable from failure, and all failures also return 0. B's length limit is `kMaxMemberDigits`, which is not defined here, so B matches A only if that constant is 2; for a larger value, inputs of 3+ digits can be accepted by B and can overflow `i32`.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 or 2 ASCII digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if the text is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
diff: They differ only in the length cap. A rejects strings longer than 2 characters, while B accepts up to 6. So for any all-digit string of 3 to 6 characters (e.g. "100", "007", "123456"), A returns false and B returns true with the parsed value. Both reject empty strings and any non-digit character, and neither can overflow i32 within its limit.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based party member number and returns false if the text isn't a number or falls outside the valid party size range.
what_b: Parses a text string into a 1-based companion slot number, returning false if the text isn't a number or falls outside 1 to kCompanionSlots.
diff: The two functions differ only in the upper bound: companionsParseMember accepts 1..kPartyMaxSize, while companionsParseSlot accepts 1..kCompanionSlots. Inputs whose parsed number n satisfies n > min(kPartyMaxSize, kCompanionSlots) but n <= max of the two give different results. For example, if kPartyMaxSize = 6 and kCompanionSlots = 4, then "5" is accepted by companionsParseMember but rejected by companionsParseSlot. Results are identical when the two constants are equal, and the lower bound (n < 1) and the parse step are identical in both.

what_a: Returns the string value stored under a given key in the session's feature-state map, or an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value stored under a constructed "hall.<k>.<field>" key in the session's feature state, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
diff: none in behaviour. Both return the stored value for the derived key, or an empty Str if absent. B takes (k, field) and derives the key internally, while A takes the key directly, so B(s, k, field) equals A(s, hallKey(k, field)).

what_a: Reinterprets a signed 32-bit integer as an unsigned 32-bit integer for indexing, with no game meaning.
what_b: Casts a signed 32-bit index to an unsigned 32-bit integer with no game meaning.
diff: none

what_a: Joins the words of a string vector from index `from` onward into a single space-separated string.
what_b: Joins the words of a typed command from a given index onward into a single string separated by single spaces.
diff: none

what_a: Looks up the display name of a quest guild from a name table by its enum index, returning an empty string if the index is out of range.
what_b: Looks up the display name for a guild by converting the Guild enum value to an integer index into a name table and returning that string.
diff: For out-of-range guild values (idx < 0 or idx >= kGuildCount), A returns an empty Str while B indexes kGuildNames out of bounds, which is undefined behaviour. For in-range values, A reads kQuestGuildNames and B reads kGuildNames, so they differ wherever those tables disagree at the same index, which I cannot verify from these snippets.

what_a: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index, converting the signed index to unsigned to access the members container directly, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the inventory of the party member at the given index, converting the signed index to unsigned for container access; it has no game meaning of its own.
diff: They return different types from different containers: `memberAt(p, i)` returns `p.members[i]` as `Character&`, and `invAt(p, i)` returns `p.inventories[i]` as `Inventory&`. They cannot be swapped at any call site because the return type and the referenced data differ for every input. Both share the same unchecked `static_cast<u32>(i)` indexing, so a negative `i` wraps to a huge index in each.

what_a: Joins the words of a token list from a given index onward into a single string separated by spaces, used to rebuild a spell name or id from the typed command's remaining words.
what_b: Joins the words of a typed command from a given index onward into a single string separated by single spaces.
diff: none

what_a: Counts how many entries on the store shelf have a given alignment, returning the tally as an integer.
what_b: Counts how many entries in the store vector share the same item id and alignment as the given item, returning that tally as the shelf count.
diff: A counts every shelf entry whose alignment equals `align`, regardless of item id. B counts only entries whose id and alignment both match `it`. Example: store = [sword(GOOD), shield(GOOD)]. A(store, GOOD) returns 2, but B(store, sword) returns 1. They agree only when every matching-alignment entry shares the target's id (or the store is empty).

what_a: Returns the string value stored under a given key in the session's feature-state map, or an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
diff: When `key` is present in `s.featureState`, both return the stored value. When `key` is absent, A returns an empty `Str`, while B returns `dflt`. The two only agree on absent keys when `dflt` is empty. A is B with `dflt = Str()`, so A can be replaced by B with an added argument, but B cannot be replaced by A at call sites that pass a non-empty default.

what_a: Returns a reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, by converting the coordinates to a cell index.
what_b: Returns a read-only reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, converting the coordinates to a flat index via cellOf.
diff: Both index `floor.squares` with the same `cellOf(x, y)`, so they return the same square for the same coordinates. They differ in constness: A takes a non-const `FloorState&` and returns a mutable `SquareState&`, so it works for writes. B takes a `const FloorState&` and returns `const SquareState&`, so it accepts const floors but its result cannot be modified. A call site that writes through the result of a non-const floor fails to compile if switched to B. A call site with a const floor fails to compile with A.

what_a: Returns a read-only reference to the party member at index i, converting the signed index to unsigned for the members array lookup without any game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by converting the signed index to an unsigned value and indexing the party's member array, with no game rule applied.
diff: Both compute `members[static_cast<u32>(i)]` with no bounds check, so they return the same element for every index. They differ in constness: A takes `const Party&` and returns `const Character&`, so it accepts const parties and forbids writes through the result. B takes `Party&` and returns `Character&`, so it rejects a const `Party` at compile time and allows mutation. Call sites that only read a member behave identically, but call sites that modify the character or pass a const party cannot be swapped without changing the signature.

what_a: Joins the words of a typed command from index `from` onward into a single string separated by spaces, which lets a multi-word guild name be passed as one argument.
what_b: Joins the words of a typed command from a given index onward into a single string separated by single spaces.
diff: They differ only when the words at or after `from` include empty strings at the start. With w = {"v", "", "x"} and from = 1, A returns "x" and B returns " x". With w = {"v", "", ""} and from = 1, A returns "" and B returns " ".

what_a: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a 1-based party member number, returning 0 if the input is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
diff: For any valid all-digit input of 1 to 6 characters, both return the same value (e.g. "42" gives 42 in both). They differ in failure signalling: A returns false and leaves `out` untouched on bad input, while B returns 0. So for "0" A reports success with value 0, but B returns 0 with no way to tell it apart from an error. For invalid input such as "", "x1", "1234567" or "-5", A returns false and B returns 0. If kMaxMemberDigits is not 6, the accepted lengths also differ, but that constant's value isn't shown.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal string representation, prefixing a minus sign for negatives, with no game meaning.
diff: Only v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). There `-v` overflows in both functions, which is undefined behaviour. In practice A returns "-" (the loop never runs and it prepends the sign), while B recurses forever via `viewInt(-v)` and overflows the stack. For every other input, including 0 and all positive and negative values, both return the same decimal string.

what_a: Returns the index of the item definition in the data table whose id matches the given item's id, or -1 if none is found.
what_b: Returns the index of the first item in the item definition table whose type matches the given kind, or -1 if none does.
diff: Function A returns the index of the first item definition whose `id` equals the given item's `id`, so it looks up an item instance's definition. Function B returns the index of the first item definition whose `type` equals the integer `kind`, so it searches by category. They differ for any input where the item's id and the requested kind come from different fields. For example, if `it.id` is 5 and some earlier definition has `type` 5 but a different id, A and B return different indices. B also takes a plain kind value where A takes an `Item`, so they cannot be swapped at call sites even with an argument change.

what_a: Classifies the edge of a dungeon square in a given facing as a wall, door, secret door, or open passage, with anything off the map treated as a wall.
what_b: Maps an edge class (wall, door, secret door, or open) to its display name ("wall", "door", "secret door", "open") for the describe-square text, with "?" as a fallback for unknown values.
diff: Not interchangeable. Function A takes (floor, x, y, facing) and returns an EdgeClass; Function B takes an EdgeClass and returns a display string ("wall", "door", "secret door", "open", or "?" for out-of-range values). Every input to A is a different type from B's input, and B's output type is a string, not an EdgeClass.

what_a: Converts 1-based (x, y) grid coordinates into an index in the flat square array of a floor, returning a pointer to that square or nullptr if the coordinates or index fall outside the map.
what_b: Returns a pointer to the square at 1-based coordinates (x, y) in a floor's row-major square array, or nullptr if the coordinates fall outside the 30-wide map or past the end of the stored squares.
diff: Results differ whenever kMapWidth != kViewMapWidth (for example, (x=1, y=2) maps to index kMapWidth in A and kViewMapWidth in B), and B returns a const pointer to a const floor while A returns a mutable pointer to a non-const floor, so call sites that write through the result cannot switch to B. If the two constants are equal (the comment in B says 30), the index math and bounds checks are identical for all inputs.

what_a: Rounds a double to four decimal places using half-even rounding and returns it as a 64-bit fixed-point integer, with no game meaning of its own.
what_b: Rounds a double to the nearest integer using round-half-to-even (banker's rounding) and returns it as an i64, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: Read literally, B(x) and A(x) differ for every nonzero input because A scales by 10000 first. Examples: x=0.5 gives A=5000 and B=0; x=1.0 gives A=10000 and B=1; x=2.5 gives A=25000 and B=2; x=-2.5 gives A=-25000 and B=-2. Assuming `roundHalfEven` implements the same half-even rule as B (its body isn't shown), A(x) equals B(x*10000.0) for all x, so the only difference is the scaling, which is an argument-form change. B's floor-based logic is correct for negative values and exact tie-breaking, so the two agree on rule and on their own domain.

what_a: Scans the game's floor table for the entry whose level number matches the requested level and returns a pointer to it, or null if none exists.
what_b: Scans the game data's item list for the entry whose id matches the given id and returns a pointer to it, or null if none matches.
diff: floorDefByLevel(data, level) returns the FloorDef whose levelNum equals the requested level, or nullptr if none matches. findItemDef(data, id) returns the ItemDef whose id equals the requested id, or nullptr if none matches. Both search a list by a key field and return a pointer or nullptr, but they search different collections (data.floors by levelNum vs. data.items by id) and return different types (FloorDef vs. ItemDef), so they cannot be substituted for each other at any call site.

what_a: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
what_b: Maps the Align enum (Good, Neutral, Evil) to its display string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
diff: Different purposes and parameter types: guildName takes a Guild and returns guild names ("Nomad" through "Healer"), while alignName takes an Align and returns "Good", "Neutral", or "Evil". Neither can replace the other at any call site, and no input is valid for both.

what_a: Clears the pending seer person offer (its kind, name, and level) from the session's feature state once the offer has been answered.
what_b: Records a pending "person" encounter offer from the seer in the feature state, storing the offered person's name and level so the offer can be answered later.
diff: For every input, the resulting `s.featureState` differs. A removes the kind, name, and level keys, leaving them absent. B sets all three keys, to "person", `name`, and `std::to_string(level)`. B also takes `name` and `level` parameters that A ignores.

what_a: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string, returning the fallback value if the string is empty, contains a non-digit character, or exceeds 1,000,000.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: none

what_a: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string, returning the fallback value if the string is empty, contains a non-digit character, or exceeds 1,000,000.
what_b: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string without throwing exceptions, returning false for empty, non-numeric, or out-of-range (above 1,000,000) input.
diff: For valid decimal strings in 0..1000000 both return the same value, assuming `accParseInt` is a plain digit parser (its body is not shown). On empty, non-digit, or >1000000 input, A returns the caller's `fallback`, while B returns false and leaves `out` unchanged, so a caller of B must supply its own default. If `accParseInt` accepts signs or whitespace, B differs further, since A rejects them.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 6 decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, returning false if any character is not a digit or the string is empty or too long.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a 1-based party member number, returning 0 if the input is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
diff: For inputs "0", "00", and "000000" (all digits, length 1 to 6, value zero), A returns true with out=0, but B returns 0, which is also what B returns for every invalid input (empty, non-digit, or too long), so the two cases can't be told apart. For empty, non-digit, or over-length inputs, A returns false and leaves out unchanged, while B returns 0. B's length cap is kMaxMemberDigits, whose value isn't shown; if it isn't 6, inputs of 7 or more digits (or fewer, if it is smaller) are accepted or rejected differently.

what_a: Linear search over the game's floor list that returns a pointer to the floor whose dungeon level matches the given level, or null if none does.
what_b: Linear search through the game's item list that returns a pointer to the item definition whose id matches the given id, or null if none exists.
diff: They search different collections (`s.game.floors` vs. `data.items`) by different fields (`dungeonLevel` vs. `id`) and return different types (`FloorState*` vs. `const ItemDef*`). Neither can stand in for the other, even with changed arguments.

what_a: Reads a numeric field from a JSON object by key, returning its value as a double or 0.0 if the key is absent.
what_b: Reads a boolean field by key from a JSON object, returning false if the key is missing.
diff: They return different types and read through different accessors, so results differ for every present key: getd returns `v->asDouble()` (e.g. 2.5 for a numeric 2.5) and getb returns `v->asBool()` (true or false). For a missing key, getd yields 0.0 and getb yields false. Neither can replace the other at a call site without changing the result type.

what_a: Rolls a quest for a guild member at the given guild level, returning none, a let-off, a defeat quest, or a fetch quest based on the SRD's quest percentages and level thresholds.
what_b: At a new guild level, rolls whether the player gets a quest (or is let off), then assigns a defeat-a-monster or fetch-an-item target from the quest tier.
diff: A returns a roll outcome code (kRollNone, kRollLetOff, kRollDefeat or kRollFetch) and changes nothing else except consuming Rnd draws. B returns void and mutates the membership: it clears the quest, calls A, emits "guilds.quest_let_off" or "guilds.quest_fetch" messages, picks a monster or item target, and sets quest.kind, target, level and state. For any input where A returns a non-None roll, B's result (membership state and messages) differs from A's (the returned code), and the return types differ.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its plain decimal string form, with a leading minus for negatives, without relying on the standard library's number formatting.
diff: none

what_a: Parses a string of decimal digits with an optional leading minus sign into a 32-bit integer, returning false if the text is malformed or the magnitude exceeds 1,000,000,000.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: A accepts a leading '-' and returns the negative value (e.g. "-5" gives -5, "-0" gives 0), while B rejects any '-'. A's upper bound is 1000000000 and B's is 1000000, so inputs such as "1000001" through "1000000000" succeed in A and fail in B. Both accept unsigned inputs up to 1000000 with identical results, and both reject empty strings, "-" alone, "+5", and non-digit characters.

what_a: Reads an integer field `k` from a JSON object `o`, returning it as an i32 or 0 if the key is missing.
what_b: Reads a numeric field from a JSON object by key, returning its value as a double or 0.0 if the key is absent.
diff: Both look up key `k` and return 0 when it is absent, but they produce different types. A returns `i32` via `asInt()`, B returns `double` via `asDouble()`. For a present value of 2.5, A gives 2 and B gives 2.5. For an integer above the i32 range (e.g. 3000000000), A truncates or wraps while B returns the full value. A's result is an integer and B's can be fractional, so B cannot replace A at call sites without changing the types and values seen there.

what_a: Formats a signed Currency amount (1/10000 gold units) as a decimal gold string with trailing zeros trimmed and a " gold" suffix.
what_b: Formats a gold amount stored in 1/10000 gold units as a decimal string with a " gold" suffix, omitting the fractional part when it is zero.
diff: They agree on non-negative amounts with no trailing zeros in the fraction (0 → "0 gold", 10000 → "1 gold", 10005 → "1.0005 gold"). They differ when the fraction has trailing zeros: 15000 gives "1.5 gold" in A and "1.5000 gold" in B, and 10050 gives "1.005 gold" in A and "1.0050 gold" in B. They also differ for negatives. A prefixes "-" and formats the magnitude correctly (-5000 → "-0.5 gold", -15000 → "-1.5 gold"). B has no sign handling and its digit extraction breaks on a negative remainder: -5000 → "0.+000 gold", -15000 → "-1.+000 gold", -1 → "0.000/ gold".

what_a: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string without throwing exceptions, returning false for empty, non-numeric, or out-of-range (above 1,000,000) input.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: Both accept plain digit strings in 0..1000000 and reject empty, non-digit, and out-of-range input. Their results can differ for inputs that depend on `accParseInt`, whose source isn't provided. If `accParseInt` accepts a leading sign, A returns true for "+5" and for "-0" (out=0), while B rejects both. If `accParseInt` doesn't guard against i64 overflow, A can wrap on very long digit strings and accept some values B rejects, while B stops as soon as the running value passes 1000000. diff: For every i32 value both return identical decimal text, including INT32_MIN ("-2147483648"). They differ for i64 inputs outside the i32 range, which B cannot accept without a narrowing cast that truncates them, and for v = INT64_MIN, where A negates with signed overflow (undefined behaviour) and returns "-" while the correct text is "-9223372036854775808". B has no equivalent of that bug because it widens to i64 before negating.

what_a: Joins the words of a token list from a given index onward into a single string separated by spaces, used to rebuild a spell name or id from the typed command's remaining words.
what_b: Joins the words of a typed command from index `from` onward into a single string separated by spaces, which lets a multi-word guild name be passed as one argument.
diff: Results differ only when an empty string appears in `w[from..]`. A separates by position (`i > from`), so it keeps a leading space for an empty first word: `w = {"verb", "", "x"}`, `from = 1` gives `" x"` in A and `"x"` in B. Likewise, `{"verb", "", ""}` gives `"  "` (two spaces) in A and `""` in B. For inputs with no empty words, including `from >= w.size()`, both return the same string.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Parses a decimal integer from text, accepting an optional leading minus sign and stopping at the first non-digit, returning 0 for unreadable input.
diff: For any input with a non-digit after an optional leading '-' that is preceded by at least one digit, A returns 0 and B returns the leading digits: "12abc" (A=0, B=12), "3.7" (A=0, B=3), "-12x" (A=0, B=-12), "5 " (A=0, B=5). A also sets ok=false for these, while B has no ok output at all. Inputs that are entirely digits (with optional '-'), or that have no leading digits such as "", "-", "abc", "+5", and "-x", give the same result in both (0, or the signed value).

what_a: Reads a boolean field by key from a JSON object, returning false if the key is missing.
what_b: Looks up a string-valued key in a JSON object and returns its string value, or an empty string if the key is missing.
diff: They return different types (bool vs Str), so they cannot be swapped at any call site. Both look up key k and return a default when it is missing (false for getb, empty string for gets). Their handling of a present key with the wrong JSON type depends on asBool and asString, which are not shown.

what_a: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's featureState map for the seer's pending person offer, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
diff: When `key` is present, both return the stored value and the results match. When `key` is absent, A returns `dflt` and B returns an empty `Str()`, so they differ whenever `dflt` is non-empty (e.g., `storedOr(s, "k", "x")` yields `"x"` but `seerGet(s, "k")` yields `""`). A can replace B by passing `""` as the third argument; B cannot replace A at call sites that pass a non-empty default.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 6 decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, returning false if any character is not a digit or the string is empty or too long.
what_b: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
diff: They differ on any input with 5 or 6 digits. For example, "12345" and "999999" return true and set out in A but return false in B, and "00000" returns true in A but false in B. Inputs of 1 to 4 digits, empty strings, and strings with non-digit characters behave identically, and neither can overflow i32.

what_a: Decides whether a guild of a given level, teaching a school at a given rate, can reach a spell of a given level, by requiring the guild to be joined and the rate to be positive and checking that spell level times rate does not exceed half the guild level plus 0.5.
what_b: Decides whether a caster can reach a given spell through any guild they have joined at level 1 or higher, checking that the guild's spell rate for the spell's school is positive, its ceiling covers the spell level, and the reach formula passes.
diff: A is a single-guild predicate on (spellLevel, rate, guildLevel); B loops over all guilds and additionally requires `m.joined` and `spellMax[school] >= spell.level`, so results differ when, for example, spellLevel=3, rate=1.0, guildLevel=10 with spellMax[school]=2: A returns true (3 <= 5.5), B returns false; or when the guild has guildLevel=10 but `joined` is false: A returns true, B returns false.

what_a: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index, converting the signed index to unsigned to access the members container directly, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by casting the signed index to unsigned and indexing the party's members array, with no game rule applied.
diff: Both return `members[static_cast<u32>(i)]` with no bounds check, so they return the same element for every input. They differ only in constness: A takes `Party&` and returns `Character&`, so a caller can mutate through the result, which B's `const` return forbids. Conversely, A cannot be called with a `const Party` at all, while B accepts one. So B cannot replace A at any call site that writes to the returned character, and A cannot replace B where the argument is const.

what_a: Resolves a player's typed guild argument, either a numeric index or a guild name compared case-insensitively, to a valid guild index for the guild log command, returning false if no valid guild matches.
what_b: Parses a typed word as either a numeric index or a case-insensitive name into a Guild enum value, returning false if neither matches a valid guild.
diff: (1) Surrounding whitespace: " 2", "Warrior " and similar inputs are trimmed by A but not by B, so A accepts them and B rejects them (unless parseNum/lowered happen to strip whitespace, which the shown code does not indicate). (2) Upper-case names: A lowercases both the input and each stored name, so "WARRIOR" matches under A; B lowercases only the input and compares it to kGuildNames, so it matches only if those constants are already lowercase. (3) Valid index range: A bounds-checks against the session's glGuildCount(s), while B bounds-checks against the constant kGuildCount, so an index in [session count, kGuildCount) is accepted by B and rejected by A if the two counts differ. (4) Name source: A reads names via glGuildName(s, i), B reads kGuildNames, so any mismatch between those sources changes results. (5) Numeric parsing: glParseInt on the trimmed, lowercased string and parseNum on the raw string may disagree on forms such as "+3" or "0x2"; I could not verify this since neither helper is shown.

what_a: Looks up a string value stored under a constructed "hall.<k>.<field>" key in the session's feature state, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a stored record field (for a given kind and name, such as a monster or item entry) in the session's feature state and returns its string value, or an empty string if it is absent.
diff: Both return the stored string at a session key or an empty string when the key is absent, but they look up different key spaces. A builds its key with `hallKey(k, field)` from an integer `k`. B builds `kRecordPrefix + kind + "." + name + "." + field` from two strings. Neither can substitute for the other at call sites, even with changed argument forms, because the same arguments would not reach the same stored entry.

what_a: Reports whether a monster group in the current encounter is still standing, meaning it has at least one living member, and returns false for any out-of-range group index.
what_b: Returns the index of the first living monster in group `gi` of an encounter (the one with hits above zero), or -1 if the group index is invalid or no member is still alive.
diff: Return type differs: A returns bool, B returns an index (i32), with -1 for none. As a predicate, B's result is wrong when the front living monster is at index 0, since 0 reads as false. The two can also disagree when `groups[g].livingCount` is inconsistent with the `monsters[i].hits` values in the group's range: A is true when livingCount > 0 even if no monster has hits > 0, and B is non-negative when some monster has hits > 0 even if livingCount is 0. B also returns -1 for g out of range where A returns false, but both give the same answer for valid g in the normal case.

what_a: Finds the index of the first monster whose LevelFound is at or above a given tier (the R51 rule for choosing monsters by level), or returns -1 if no monster qualifies.
what_b: Finds the index of the last monster in the monster table whose floor is at or above the given tier's threshold, marking where the monster list for that tier ends (SRD R51), returning -1 if the first monster is already deeper than the tier.
diff: Different predicates and return values. A returns the first index with levelFound >= tier, or -1. B returns (first index with monsterFloorOf(mon) > tier) - 1, or count-1 if none is deeper. Examples: levels [1,2,3], tier 0: A returns 0, B returns -1. Levels [1,2], tier 5: A returns -1, B returns 1. Levels [1,2,3], tier 2 gives A=1 and B=1 only by coincidence if monsterFloorOf matches levelFound, which the code does not show.

what_a: Parses the player's typed "seer" command, showing usage help, answering the Seer's pending offer with yes or no, or dispatching a paid search for a creature, item, or person.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "seer" command, which lets the player search for a creature, item, or person for a fee, and answer yes or no to a pending offer.
diff: Function A handles a player's "seer" input and returns a bool with a reply string, while Function B returns void and only registers the command. They cannot be swapped at any call site, and no input makes them produce the same result.

what_a: Looks up the display name for a guild by converting the Guild enum value to an integer index into a name table and returning that string.
what_b: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
diff: For every valid `Guild` value, the two functions agree only if `kGuildNames[i]` holds the same string as the literal in B's matching case. That table isn't visible here, so this can't be confirmed. For an out-of-range enum value, A indexes past the array (undefined behaviour), while B returns `"?"`.

what_a: Builds the text of a library item page for the player, listing the item's abilities when the entry is fully known and otherwise showing "Not everything is known."
what_b: Handles the player's typed "library" command, listing known library entries, searching them by name prefix, or showing the page for a monster or item entry, and returns the text reply.
diff: They serve different purposes and cannot substitute for each other at any call site. itemPage(s, e) takes one entry and returns its page text, with an "Abilities:" line at grade >= kLibEverything and "Not everything is known." otherwise. cmdLibrary(s, w, reply) takes a tokenized command, returns bool, and writes to reply. It lists all names, runs a prefix search, or looks up a monster or item by name, and it reports usage or no-match errors. For a single selected entry it delegates to pageFor, which is not itemPage.

what_a: Returns the pack item at a given member and slot, or nullptr if the slot is the hands (slot 1), out of range, or empty (id ≤ 0).
what_b: Scans the pack inventory from slot 1 upward (skipping the Hands slot at 0) and returns the index of the first slot whose item id is 0, or -1 if the pack is full.
diff: Not replaceable at any call site. realignItemAt(s, member1, slot1) returns an Item* for an occupied pack slot >= 2 of a member, or nullptr otherwise. starterFreeSlot(inv) returns the index of the first empty pack slot scanning from 1, or -1. For example, realignItemAt returns nullptr for slot 1 and for any empty slot, while starterFreeSlot returns 1 when pack[1] is empty, and it takes an Inventory rather than a Session and member.

what_a: Returns the first pack slot (slots 2 through kPackSlots, skipping the Hands slot) of a party member that holds no item, or nullptr if the pack is full.
what_b: Returns the pack item at a given member and slot, or nullptr if the slot is the hands (slot 1), out of range, or empty (id ≤ 0).
diff: They return opposite results for the same occupied or empty slot. A returns a pointer only when the slot holds an empty item (id <= 0) and scans slots 2..kPackSlots for the first such slot. B returns a pointer only when the specified slot holds an occupied item (id > 0), and it checks one given slot. For an empty slot, A returns that slot's pointer and B returns nullptr. For an occupied slot, B returns the item and A skips it. For a full pack, A returns nullptr and B returns the item in the requested slot.

what_a: Reports whether a monster group in the current encounter is still standing, meaning it has at least one living member, and returns false for any out-of-range group index.
what_b: Reports whether a monster group still has at least one living member, which the game's melee rules (R2, R3, R5) use to decide if the group keeps fighting.
diff: For any in-range index, groupStanding(game, g) equals groupStanding(game.encounter.groups[g]). The exception is an out-of-range index (g < 0 or g >= kMaxGroups): Function A returns false, while Function B has no index to receive and would need a call site that indexes first, which is undefined behaviour for such g.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer from text, accepting an optional leading minus sign and stopping at the first non-digit, returning 0 for unreadable input.
what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: Empty string: A returns 0, B returns false. "-" alone: A returns 0, B returns false. Any trailing or non-digit junk ("12abc", "3 4", "+5", "abc"): A returns the leading digits or 0, B returns false. "--5": A returns 0, B returns false. Magnitude above 1000000000000 (e.g. "1000000000001"): A returns the value (and overflows, which is undefined behaviour, past about 19 digits), B returns false. Valid decimal inputs with an optional leading '-' and magnitude at most 10^12 give identical values.

what_a: Joins the words of a string vector from index `from` onward into a single space-separated string.
what_b: Joins the words of a typed command from index `from` onward into a single string separated by spaces, which lets a multi-word guild name be passed as one argument.
diff: They differ when the joined output is still empty at a later index, which happens when one or more leading elements w[from..] are empty strings. Example: w = {"verb", "", "x"}, from = 1 gives " x" from A and "x" from B. Another: w = {"verb", ""}, from = 1 gives "" from A and "" from B, but w = {"verb", "", ""}, from = 1 gives " " from A and "" from B.

what_a: Parses a party member number from the second word of a typed command and checks that it falls within the current party size, returning whether it is valid.
what_b: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
diff: For any valid input such as "3" with party size 4, A sets member=3 (1-based) and B sets idx=2 (0-based). A returns false when w.size()<2 and takes its input as a word list, while B takes a single string. Both reject values outside 1..party size, but A bounds with accPartySize(s) and B with s.game.party.size, which are equal only if accPartySize returns that field.

what_a: Decides whether a chest gets a magic lock by checking whether the square allows one, then rolls the lock chance against the chest's treasure class to return the resulting ChestLock.
what_b: Generates a fight-left chest on a square by rolling its treasure class, trap, magic lock, gold (scaled by group standing, lock and class), and chest items, storing the result on the chest.
diff: Every input differs in effect. A returns a `ChestLock` computed from `squareBits`, `treasureClass`, and `lockedChance`, with no side effects. B returns `void` and mutates `chest`: it clears the trap, sets or clears `hasChest`/`chestClass`/`chestItems`/`chestGold`, stores trap, lock, and gold on the square, and spawns items. B also rolls the treasure class and returns early when it is `kTreasureClassNone`, where A never does. A is only the lock step inside B's pass (`applyMagicLock` is called at R10 in B).

what_a: Returns a reference to the inventory of the party member at the given index, converting the signed index to unsigned for container access; it has no game meaning of its own.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by converting the signed index to an unsigned value and indexing the party's member array, with no game rule applied.
diff: Return types differ (`Inventory&` vs `Character&`), so neither can replace the other at any call site. A reads `p.inventories`, B reads `party.members`, so the same index selects different data. Both perform the same unchecked `static_cast<u32>` index, so a negative `i` wraps to a huge index in each and is out of bounds in both.

what_a: Looks up a race's base resistance to a given damage kind from the race table, returning 0 if the race or resistance entry is missing, as the first step of the game's resistance calculation.
what_b: Returns the resistance value a creature gets from its gear, which is a flat 90 when the item grants resistance and otherwise the race's base resistance, with gear not stacking.
diff: Function A returns the race's base resistance value for the damage kind (or 0 if the race or entry is missing), while Function B ignores any race data and returns 90 whenever itemResists is true, and otherwise returns the raceBase passed in. For example, with itemResists=false and raceBase=40, B returns 40 but A would return the race's own value for that kind; with itemResists=true, B returns 90 regardless of the race, while A never returns 90 unless the data table says so.

what_a: Returns the pack item at a given member and slot, or nullptr if the slot is the hands (slot 1), out of range, or empty (id ≤ 0).
what_b: Refuses a pack slot of 1 (the hands, not an item) by setting the player-facing reply "Slot 1 is your hands, not an item." and returning false, otherwise accepting the slot.
diff: Their outputs and purposes don't match. realignItemAt returns an Item* (nullptr for slot1 < 2, for an out-of-range or empty slot, or for id <= 0) and gives no message. gearSlotOk returns a bool and sets a reply string, refusing only kFirstPackSlot. For example, slot1 = 1 gives nullptr from A and false from B, and slot1 = 0 gives nullptr from A but true from B. For an empty slot 5, A returns nullptr while B returns true.

what_a: Formats a 64-bit integer as a decimal string, with no game meaning.
what_b: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal text string, handling zero and negative values, with no game meaning.
diff: Only at v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). Function A returns "-9223372036854775808". Function B negates v, which overflows (undefined behaviour). In practice it wraps back to INT64_MIN, so the recursion never terminates and the call overflows the stack. For every other i64 value, including 0, positive values, and other negatives, the outputs match.

what_a: Converts a 1-based player slot number to a 0-based pack index by subtracting one, with no game rule applied beyond the slot numbering convention.
what_b: Converts a 0-based pack index into a 1-based player slot number by adding one, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: packIndexFromPlayerSlot(n) returns n - 1 and playerSlotFromPackIndex(n) returns n + 1, so they are inverses of each other, not equivalent. For every input, the results differ (e.g. playerSlot 1 maps to pack index 0, but pack index 0 maps to player slot 1 only through the other function; applying the same function to the same input gives 0 for A(1) versus 2 for B(1)).

what_a: Returns the first pack slot (slots 2 through kPackSlots, skipping the Hands slot) of a party member that holds no item, or nullptr if the pack is full.
what_b: Scans the pack inventory from slot 1 upward (skipping the Hands slot at 0) and returns the index of the first slot whose item id is 0, or -1 if the pack is full.
diff: (1) Empty test: A treats any item with id <= 0 as free, so a slot holding a negative id is free in A but occupied in B (B requires id == 0). (2) Return convention: A returns an Item* or nullptr, while B returns an internal index or -1, so call sites must change even though the argument form can match. (3) Argument form: A takes Session& and a 1-based member, while B takes const Inventory&. Assuming accPackItem's 1-based slot k maps to internal index k-1, both scan the same pack range (indices 1..kPackSlots-1) with Hands excluded.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based party member number and returns false if the text isn't a number or falls outside the valid party size range.
what_b: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
diff: (1) Output value: for every accepted input k, A sets member1 = k while B sets idx = k-1 (e.g. "1" gives member1 = 1 in A and idx = 0 in B). (2) Upper bound: A accepts up to the constant kPartyMaxSize, while B accepts only up to s.game.party.size, so with a party of 2, "3" returns true in A (member1 = 3) and false in B. (3) The underlying parsers differ (companionsParseNumber into i32 vs. parseNum into i64), and their handling of malformed or overflowing text is not shown, so those inputs may also differ.

what_a: Computes a character's creation point pool for the Mordor game by starting from 30, adding the race's bonus points, and subtracting the points already spent on base attributes above the race's minimums.
what_b: Returns how many character-creation points remain for a race and its six stats, computed by the rules module as a 30-point pool plus the race's bonus points minus the stats' amounts above the race minimums.
diff: none in behaviour. B takes a Session and a fixed `Arr<i32, 6>`, while A takes a Ctx and `Arr<i32, kStatCount>`. Those are argument-form differences only, and they hold only if kStatCount is 6.

what_a: Builds the one-line "x,y,level facing [ n ]" readout for the Look page, appending "+d" to the living count when dead characters are present in the party's location.
what_b: Builds the text of the Look page for the player, showing the readout line, the current square's description, messages about dead bodies and other characters in the room, and a table of the characters present with their name, guild, level and hits.
diff: For every input, lookText returns a multi-line Look page that includes readoutLine's output as its first line, plus the square line, the body and stranger messages, and the row table. readoutLine returns only the single readout line, so the two never produce the same result. The only shared content is that first line.

what_a: Returns true when every field of an Area record is at its zeroed default, meaning the area has no stamp, emptied time, respawn timer, lair, spawn mask, or fight state.
what_b: Serializes or deserializes one dungeon floor's state (level, tallies, room counts, square explored/identified/seen bits, and area respawn data such as emptied time, respawn timer, lair and spawn mask) to or from the save file.
diff: Function A is a pure predicate that returns true when all six Area fields are zero. Function B is a void save/load routine that writes or reads the FloorState's dungeon level, tallies, square bit rows, and area rows through an Io object. They have different return types, side effects, and purposes, so no input yields the same result from both.

what_a: Builds the string key "quest.<member>.<guild>" used to store an open-quest flag for a given member and guild in featureState.
what_b: Reports whether a given party member has an open quest for a guild by checking the session's feature state for that quest key being set to "1".
diff: Return types differ: A returns a string key (e.g. "quest.3.1"), while B returns a bool, true only when the session's featureState contains that key with the value "1". No input gives the same result from both, so neither can replace the other.

what_a: Returns the string value stored under a given key in the session's feature-state map, or an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a stored record field (for a given kind and name, such as a monster or item entry) in the session's feature state and returns its string value, or an empty string if it is absent.
diff: A looks up its key verbatim, while B looks up `kRecordPrefix + kind + "." + name + "." + field`. They agree only when A's key equals that composed string, so `A(s, key)` and `B(s, kind, name, field)` disagree for most inputs, e.g. `A(s, "foo")` vs `B(s, "", "foo", "")`.

what_a: Converts a 1-based item alignment value (Good, Neutral, Evil) into a 0-based pen index by subtracting one.
what_b: Maps a pen alignment index (0, 1, or 2) to its display name for the confinement pens: Good, Neutral, or Evil, with any value other than 0 or 1 treated as Evil.
diff: Different return types and input domains. A maps an ItemAlign enum (Good=1, Neutral=2, Evil=3) to a 0-based pen index, returning an i32. B maps a 0-based pen index to a name, returning a Str. For example, A(Good) = 0 and A(Evil) = 2, while B(0) = "Good", B(1) = "Neutral", and B(2) or any other value = "Evil". A cannot replace B or the reverse at any call site.

what_a: Reports whether a seer (the person-offer feature) currently has a pending offer stored in the session's feature state, which the game uses to track an offer until the player answers it.
what_b: Records a pending "person" encounter offer from the seer in the feature state, storing the offered person's name and level so the offer can be answered later.
diff: A is a read-only query that returns whether `featureState[kSeerKindKey]` exists and is non-empty, and it never modifies the session. B is a void mutator that writes "person", the name, and the level into `featureState`. They cannot be substituted for each other at any call site; they differ in return type (bool vs. void) and in side effects (none vs. writes three keys).

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Converts an integer to its decimal string form, with no game meaning.
diff: For every i32 value both produce the same decimal string (including 0 and negatives). They differ for i64 values outside the i32 range: A prints them correctly, but B's i32 parameter truncates them, so replacing A's call sites with B gives wrong output. A also has undefined behaviour for INT64_MIN, since `-v` overflows, but B cannot receive that value.

what_a: Returns a race's experience factor from the race table, which the game uses as a multiplier when computing experience gains for characters of that race.
what_b: Computes the threshold experience points needed for a character at level x, scaled by the guild's experience factor and the race's experience multiplier, rounded to a whole number (returns 0 for x ≤ 0).
diff: Not comparable. A returns one raw race-table Exp factor, a double, for a race (no guild, no x, no rounding). B computes a rounded integer threshold XP from x, guild and race. Every input where B's result is a function of a race-table lookup would also depend on x and the guild, which A does not take.

what_a: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal text representation, handling the sign and the most negative value without using the C library.
what_b: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal string representation, prefixing a minus sign for negatives, with no game meaning.
diff: Only for v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). A returns "-9223372036854775808". B computes -v, which overflows (undefined behaviour; in practice it stays negative and recurses until the stack overflows). All other inputs, including 0, positive values, and other negatives, produce identical strings.

what_a: Computes the race experience multiplier f = (ln(r)/ln(r+1)) + 1 - 0.7 + r/25 from the race's experience factor plus one, using the SRD Chapter 5 formula for scaling experience by race.
what_b: Computes the experience points a character needs to reach a given level, summing per-level thresholds from the guild and race experience factors and then applying the race experience multiplier.
diff: Not comparable as replacements. Function A returns a double race multiplier for a given r, while Function B returns an i64 XP threshold for a given level, guildExp, and raceExp. B calls A internally with r = raceExp+1, so they cannot substitute for each other at any call site, for any input.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 or 2 ASCII digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if the text is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string, returning the fallback value if the string is empty, contains a non-digit character, or exceeds 1,000,000.
diff: Signatures and failure signalling differ: A returns `bool` and writes `out` on success, while B returns `int` and returns `fallback` on failure, so a call site cannot be swapped without changing its form. Accepted inputs also differ: "007" gives A false and B 7; "100" gives A false and B 100; "123" gives A false and B 123; "1000000" gives A false and B 1000000; "1000001" gives A false and B the fallback; "" and non-digit strings give A false and B the fallback, which is only a failure signal if the caller's fallback is distinguishable from a valid parse.

what_a: Maps a wearer's alignment (Good, Neutral, or Evil) to the alignment bit that item alignment restrictions are checked against, per game rule R11.
what_b: Checks whether a guild accepts a character's alignment by testing the guild's alignment bitmask for the bit matching that alignment (Good, Neutral, or Evil), per SRD rule R15.
diff: Return types differ: A returns `u32` (`kAlignBitGood`/`kAlignBitNeutral`/`kAlignBitEvil`, or 0 for an out-of-range value), while B returns `bool`. A ignores its guild argument and maps an alignment to its bit, while B tests whether a guild's `alignMask` includes that alignment's bit, so for any alignment A returns a nonzero bit regardless of mask and B returns false when the mask lacks that bit (e.g. `alignMask == 0`). B also has undefined behaviour for out-of-range `align` values, where `1 << a` is an invalid shift, whereas A returns 0.

what_a: Returns true if any guild that the character belongs to (in scope under the class-restriction setting) is permitted by the item's guild mask to use that item.

what_a: Returns the facing direction a character would have after turning one step clockwise (right) from their current facing, wrapping North→East→South→West→North.

what_a: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.

what_a: Builds the INI-style lookup key "option." followed by the given option name, with no game meaning of its own.

what_a: Checks whether a monster's levelFound falls within the eligibility window for a target floor, i.e. between the floor minus the spread and the floor itself (rule R12).

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.

Function B returns "-9223372036854775808". All other inputs, including 0, positive values, and every other negative value, produce identical strings.

what_a: Returns the pack item at a given member and slot, or nullptr if the slot is the hands (slot 1), out of range, or empty (id ≤ 0).
what_b: Checks whether a typed swap slot is a valid pack slot, refusing slot 1 (the hands, which never move) and any slot beyond the pack's limit.
diff: Return type differs: realignItemAt returns an Item* (or nullptr), while swapSlotInRange returns a bool. For any slot in 2..kPackSlots, swapSlotInRange returns true, but realignItemAt returns nullptr when that slot is empty (id <= 0). Slot 1, slot 0, and negative slots are rejected by both. The upper bound for realignItemAt is whatever accPackItem enforces, which isn't shown, so it may differ from kPackSlots.

what_a: Returns a race's experience factor from the race table, which the game uses as a multiplier when computing experience gains for characters of that race.
what_b: Computes the experience points a character needs to reach a given level, summing per-level thresholds from the guild and race experience factors and then applying the race experience multiplier.

what_a: Returns the index of the item definition in the data table whose id matches the given item's id, or -1 if none is found.
what_b: Scans the game data's item list for the entry whose id matches the given id and returns a pointer to it, or null if none matches.

Argument form also differs (A takes `(Ctx, Item)` and reads `it.id`; B takes `(GameData, i32)`), which the question allows.

what_a: Returns a fixed usage string describing the `use <member> <slot>` command (potions heal, scrolls cast) without doing any game work.

diff: A returns the usage string and has no side effects. B is void and registers two commands: "use" (Screen::Dungeon, cmdDungeonUse) and "useitem" (Screen::Town, cmdTownUseItem). what_a: Returns the absolute value of a 32-bit integer.
what_b: Casts a signed 32-bit index to an unsigned 32-bit integer with no game meaning.
diff: They agree only for non-negative inputs (e.g. v=5 gives 5 from both). For negative inputs they differ: duseAbs(-5) returns 5, while uidx(-5) returns 4294967291 (two's-complement reinterpretation). The return types also differ (i32 vs u32), and duseAbs(INT_MIN) is undefined behaviour from signed overflow, while uidx(INT_MIN) returns 2147483648.

what_a: Formats a gold amount stored in 1/10000 gold units as a decimal string with a " gold" suffix, omitting the fractional part when it is zero.
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold currency amount as a decimal gold string with a minus sign for negatives and four fractional digits zero-padded.
diff: (1) A appends " gold" to every result and B never does, so results differ for every input (e.g. 15000 gives "1.5000" from B and "1.5000 gold" from A; the frac-is-nonzero case also differs by that suffix alone). (2) Zero fraction: units=50000 gives "5.0000" from B and "5 gold" from A, since A omits the decimal point and B always keeps it. (3) Negatives: units=-5 gives "-0.0005" from B, but A computes whole=0 and frac=-5, so it emits non-digit characters (e.g. '+') in the output. (4) Units with a nonzero fraction are otherwise formatted identically (4-digit zero-padded fraction, e.g. 10 gives "0.0010" in B and "0.0010 gold" in A).

what_a: Linear search over the game's floor list that returns a pointer to the floor whose dungeon level matches the given level, or null if none does.

what_a: Linear search over the game's floor list that returns a pointer to the floor whose dungeon level matches the given level, or null if none does.

what_a: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
what_b: Converts a 0-based pack index into a 1-based player slot number by adding one, with no game meaning of its own.

B takes a 0-based pack index and returns a 1-based slot (packIndex+1) with no parsing, validation, or failure path. For example, A("3") yields idx 2 with true, while B(2) yields 3.

what_a: Parses the typed "give" command, dispatching "give gold" and "give item" to their handlers and replying with usage text when the subcommand is missing or unrecognized.

what_a: Scans the game's floor table for the entry whose level number matches the requested level and returns a pointer to it, or null if none exists.

what_a: Looks up a race's base resistance to a given damage kind from the race table, returning 0 if the race or resistance entry is missing, as the first step of the game's resistance calculation.
what_b: Tests whether an item's resistance bitmask grants resistance to a given damage kind, returning false for out-of-range kinds.

B returns a bool from `(resistanceFlags & kItemResistBits[idx]) != 0`, or false when the index is out of range. what_a: Converts a 1-based (x, y) map coordinate into a single linear square index by row-major arithmetic on the map width.
what_b: Converts a 2D map coordinate (x, y) into a flat array index by row-major order using the map's side length.
diff: For every (x, y), A(x, y) = x + 30(y−1) and B(x, y) = x + kMapSide·y. If kMapSide = 30 (not confirmed; the constant is not in the excerpts), B(x, y) − A(x, y) = 30 for all inputs, so results differ everywhere. For any other kMapSide, the gap is y·(kMapSide − 30) + 30, which also varies with y. Example: A(1,1) = 1, while B(1,1) = 31 if kMapSide = 30.

what_a: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string, returning the fallback value if the string is empty, contains a non-digit character, or exceeds 1,000,000.
diff: A returns false and B returns `fallback` for the same bad inputs, so callers must handle failure differently. Value differences: `"0000001"` gives A false and B 1 (A rejects length > 6 before parsing, B only bounds the numeric value). `"1000000"` gives A false and B 1000000 (B's bound is inclusive at 1000000, A's is 999999). Strings of 7+ characters with value ≤ 1000000 (e.g., `"0000000"`, `"0000042"`) are rejected by A and accepted by B. Empty and non-digit inputs both fail in each, but via different signals.

what_a: Reinterprets a signed 32-bit integer as an unsigned 32-bit integer for indexing, with no game meaning.
what_b: Returns the absolute value of a 32-bit integer.
diff: For nonnegative i the two agree in value (e.g. 5 gives 5), but the return types differ (u32 vs i32). For negative i they diverge: uidx(-1) = 4294967295 while duseAbs(-1) = 1. For i = INT_MIN, uidx gives 2147483648 while duseAbs overflows in signed negation (undefined behaviour).

what_a: Returns a character's natural maximum spell points by feeding their base Intelligence and Wisdom stats into the casting formula maxSpellPoints.
what_b: Computes a character's maximum spell points from their natural Intelligence and Wisdom, using a provisional formula of (INT + WIS) × 5 that the SRD part does not state.
diff: none. A takes an `Abilities` and B takes two ints, but that is an argument-form difference, and for any Int/Wis pair A returns exactly what B returns.

what_a: Handles the player's typed up or down stairs command in the dungeon by checking whether stairs are on the party's square, moving the party to the adjacent level (or back to town from level 1), and setting the reply message shown to the player.
what_b: Handles the town "descend" command by moving the party from town into dungeon level 1 at the up-stairs square, setting each member's location and facing, and producing the arrival message.
diff: A moves the party one level up or down from a staircase the party is standing on, and B enters dungeon level 1 from town. Inputs where results differ: (1) party in town (dungeonLevel 0): A replies "There is no such level." and B descends to level 1 if no living member and not already in the dungeon; (2) party already in the dungeon: A proceeds with the stair move, while B replies "The party is already in the dungeon."; (3) party not on any stairs square: A replies "There are no stairs here.", while B ignores position and places the party on the level-1 stairs-up square; (4) delta = +1 from a level-N stairs-down square with N below levelLimit: A moves the party down, while B is never a move between levels; (5) climb to town from level 1: A exits to town, while B has no such path; (6) no living members: B refuses, while A does not check for this; (7) effects: A calls leaveArea, markExplored, and advanceTime and sets the reply to "You descend/climb the stairs.", while B sets lost* flags, updates deepestReached and the underground clock, and sets the reply to "The party descends to dungeon level 1."

what_a: Linear search over the loaded floor definitions that returns a pointer to the floor whose levelNum matches the given dungeon level, or null if none does.
what_b: Linear search through the game's item list that returns a pointer to the item definition whose id matches the given id, or null if none exists.

Any call that finds a match in one can return a different object or nullptr in the other. For example, if `data.floors` has a floor with `levelNum` 3 and `data.items` has an item with `id` 3, A(data, 3) returns the floor and B(data, 3) returns the item. Both return nullptr when nothing matches.

what_a: Returns the pack item at a given member and slot, or nullptr if the slot is the hands (slot 1), out of range, or empty (id ≤ 0).
what_b: Checks whether a pack slot is a valid item slot (2 through kPackSlots, since slot 1 is the hands), which gates whether an item in that slot can be uncursed.
diff: Different return types and purposes. Function A returns an `Item*` (or nullptr), while B returns a `bool`. For slot 2 with an empty pack slot, A returns nullptr and B returns true. For slot 1, both reject it. For slot 41 (assuming kPackSlots is 40), B returns false, and A returns whatever accPackItem decides, which may differ from B's bound.

what_a: Returns the first pack slot (slots 2 through kPackSlots, skipping the Hands slot) of a party member that holds no item, or nullptr if the pack is full.
what_b: Checks whether a pack slot is a valid item slot (2 through kPackSlots, since slot 1 is the hands), which gates whether an item in that slot can be uncursed.
