what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: Both reject empty strings, a lone "-", non-digit characters, and "+" signs, and both accept leading zeros and "-0". They differ in the magnitude limit: B rejects any value above 1000000000000 (and below -1000000000000), while A accepts up to the i64 maximum 9223372036854775807. For example, "1000000000001" gives true from A and false from B, and "9223372036854775807" gives true from A and false from B. Values from 1000000000001 through 9223372036854775807 (and their negatives) are the only inputs where the results differ.

what_a: Reads an integer field for a pending raise (resurrection) from the session's feature state by member and field name, returning the fallback value if the key is missing or the stored text doesn't parse as an integer.
what_b: Reads an integer field `k` from a JSON object `o`, returning it as an i32 or 0 if the key is missing.
diff: They take different inputs: A takes a `Session` plus a `member`/`field` key and reads a stored string in `featureState`, while B takes a `JsonValue` and a key and reads a JSON value. On a missing key, A returns the caller's `fallback` and B returns 0. A also returns `fallback` when the stored string fails `rescueParseInt`, a step B does not have. Even with `fallback = 0`, A and B cannot be swapped at call sites because their arguments and sources differ.

what_a: Reads one of three per-square flags from a dungeon square's state (explored, identified, or seen/automapped) for save and load, with the automap flag reduced to a simple seen check.
what_b: Sets one of three per-square flags (explored, identified, or automap) on a map square's state, selected by index, with no game rule logic of its own.
diff: getBit reads a value and returns it, while setBit writes a value and returns void, so neither can replace the other at any call site. Their `which` mapping agrees (0 is explored, 1 is identified, anything else is automap), and they round-trip consistently: setBit(sq, k, v) followed by getBit(sq, k) yields v for every k.

what_a: Returns the trap chance for a chest's treasure class (0 to 3), giving 0 for any out-of-range class, as set by the game's chest trap table.
what_b: Stores a chest's treasure class, trap, lock, and gold amount onto a square's record in the game's room state, marking the square as holding a chest only when the treasure class is positive.
diff: Function A is a pure lookup that returns kTrapChanceByClass[treasureClass] for classes 0–3 and 0 otherwise, with no side effects. Function B is a void setter that mutates a SquareState, storing hasChest (true only when treasureClass > 0), the chest class, trap, lock and gold, and it returns nothing. They share an input (treasureClass) but Function A returns a trap chance value and Function B stores chest data, so they cannot substitute for each other at any call site.

what_a: Pools every other party member's on-hand gold into the selected member, reporting the amount moved, or noting that pooling stopped at a purse overflow.
what_b: Pools each other party member's on-hand gold into the selected member in index order, stopping at the first member whose full amount would exceed the selected member's currency cap.
diff: Not replaceable at any call site. `doPool` writes a player-facing message to `reply` and returns void, while `poolGoldToSelected` moves the gold and returns a bool. `doPool` delegates the pooling to `poolGoldToSelected`, so a call to `poolGoldToSelected` moves gold without producing any reply.

what_a: Returns a reference to the item's definition by indexing the game's item table directly with the item's id, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index, converting the signed index to unsigned to access the members container directly, with no game rule applied.
diff: Not interchangeable for any inputs. A takes (Ctx, Item) and returns an item definition from `ctx.data.items` indexed by `item.id`. B takes (Party, i32) and returns a character from `p.members` indexed by `i`. They read different containers and return different types.

what_a: Copies fields from a parsed JSON object into an ItemDef struct by key name, reading integers, strings, doubles, and arrays with no game logic applied.
what_b: Copies the fields of a monster definition from a parsed JSON object into a MonsterDef struct, reading each stat, flag, and item list by name from the generated data file.
diff: Function A reads ItemDef and Function B reads MonsterDef, so they populate different structs. Only six keys are read by both (tableIndex, name, att, def, id, damageMod) and they use the same helpers. Each function reads fields the other never touches (for example, A reads price, rarity, and spellId, while B reads hits, chance, and items).

what_a: Computes the spell-slot ceiling for a magic category by taking the highest SpellMax value for that category across all guilds that have a spell table.
what_b: Reports whether a spell is unreachable by a caster, which is true when the spell's level exceeds the ceiling for its category.
diff: A returns an i32 (the ceiling, 0 when no guild has a spell table), while B returns a bool (true when spell.level exceeds that ceiling). Their return types and purposes differ, so no input gives matching results; B calls A, so A is a helper for B, not an equivalent.

what_a: Copies fields from a parsed JSON object into an ItemDef struct by key name, reading integers, strings, doubles, and arrays with no game logic applied.
what_b: Copies the "areaId" and "flags" integer fields from a parsed JSON object into a FloorField struct, with no game rules applied.
diff: Not interchangeable for any input. A reads an ItemDef (about 28 fields, including string `name`, double `damageMod`, and array `statsRequired`/`statsMod`) and never touches FloorField. B reads a FloorField (`areaId`, `flags`) and never touches ItemDef. Each would leave the other's target type unset.

what_a: Checks whether the typed text names a valid pack slot (2 through kPackSlots, since slot 1 is the Hands) for a give command and returns that slot number, or -1 to signal "No Item to give!".
what_b: Returns the first pack slot (slots 2 through kPackSlots, skipping the Hands slot) of a party member that holds no item, or nullptr if the pack is full.
diff: Function A returns an `i32` slot number or -1, and Function B returns an `Item*` or nullptr, so their return types and purposes don't match. A parses user text and validates it as slot 2..kPackSlots, while B scans a member's pack for the first empty slot (id <= 0). No input makes them interchangeable.

what_a: Checks whether a pack slot is a valid item slot (2 through kPackSlots, since slot 1 is the hands), which gates whether an item in that slot can be uncursed.
what_b: Refuses a pack slot of 1 (the hands, not an item) by setting the player-facing reply "Slot 1 is your hands, not an item." and returning false, otherwise accepting the slot.
diff: Slot 1 gives false in both. Slots 2..40 give true in both. Slot 0, negative slots, and slots above kPackSlots (>40) give false in A but true in B. B also fills `reply` with a message when refusing slot 1, and A has no such output, so the signatures differ too.

what_a: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold amount as a human-readable string with up to four decimal places and trailing zeros removed, followed by " gold".
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold currency amount as a decimal gold string with a minus sign for negatives and four fractional digits zero-padded.
diff: Both convert 1/10000-gold units to a signed decimal string, but they differ for every input with a non-zero value. A appends " gold" and B does not. A drops trailing zeros and the decimal point when the fraction is zero, while B always prints four decimal places. Examples: 0 gives "0 gold" (A) vs "0.0000" (B); 120000 gives "12 gold" vs "12.0000"; 5000 gives "0.5 gold" vs "0.5000"; 12345 gives "1.2345 gold" vs "1.2345"; -5000 gives "-0.5 gold" vs "-0.5000".

what_a: Lets a party member realign an unequipped pack item to good, neutral, or evil alignment by paying a fee computed from the item's price and the number of alignment steps, then applies the change.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "realign" command, which lets the player change an item's alignment for a fee, with its usage line shown to the player.
diff: Function A validates its arguments, charges the realign fee, changes the item's alignment, and sets a reply. Function B takes no arguments, returns void, and only registers the "realign" command with the Town screen, the handler `&cmdRealign`, and the help text, so it changes no item, charges no fee, and sets no reply.

what_a: Computes a guild's attack and defence ratings by adding the base attack/defence value (kBaseAD) to the best attack and defence values the guild has, per rule R12.
what_b: Computes a character's attack rating (AttackOf) by summing the base attack value, the stat-derived attack bonus, the best guild attack bonus, and the equipped items' attack values, then clamping the result at zero.
diff: Different return types and purposes. guildAD returns an AdPair holding both att (kBaseAD + best.att) and def (kBaseAD + best.def), with no clamping. attackOf returns a single i32 equal to max(0, baseAD + statsADOf(c) + best.att + equippedAtt(ctx, inv)). guildAD never includes stats or equipment, has no floor at zero, and computes no defence value. attackOf never produces a def value.

what_a: Formats a 64-bit integer as a decimal string, with no game meaning.
what_b: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal string representation, prefixing a minus sign for negatives, with no game meaning.
diff: Only for v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). A returns "-9223372036854775808". B negates v, which overflows (undefined behaviour); in practice -v equals v, so the recursion never terminates and the call overflows the stack. For all other values, including 0 and every negative value above INT64_MIN, both return the same decimal string.

what_a: Searches a list of floor states for the one whose dungeon level matches the given level and returns its index, or -1 if none matches.
what_b: Looks up the stored floor whose dungeon level matches the party's current dungeon level, returning nullptr if no such floor is saved.
diff: Both find the first floor whose dungeonLevel matches. A takes the level as an argument and returns its index (or -1 if none); B reads the level from s.game.party.dungeonLevel and returns a pointer to the floor (or nullptr if none). So for the same floors and level, A's index i corresponds to B's &floors[i], and A's -1 corresponds to B's nullptr. Call sites would need changes beyond argument form, since the return type and the source of the level both differ.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its plain decimal string form, with a leading minus for negatives, without relying on the standard library's number formatting.
what_b: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, handling negative values and zero without any game meaning.
diff: Only v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808) differs. Function A negates it, which overflows (undefined behaviour for signed i64), and in practice the loop never runs and it returns "-". Function B returns "-9223372036854775808". All other inputs give identical strings.

what_a: Checks whether a typed swap slot is a valid pack slot, refusing slot 1 (the hands, which never move) and any slot beyond the pack's limit.
what_b: Scans the pack inventory from slot 1 upward (skipping the Hands slot at 0) and returns the index of the first slot whose item id is 0, or -1 if the pack is full.
diff: Not interchangeable at any call site. A is a bool predicate on a single slot number (true for 2 through kPackSlots, false otherwise), while B scans the inventory and returns an internal index of the first empty pack slot, or -1. Their return types and purposes differ, so no input makes them agree.

what_a: Reports whether a monster group in the current encounter is still standing, meaning it has at least one living member, and returns false for any out-of-range group index.
what_b: Returns true while any encounter group still has living monsters, so the combat round continues, and returns false once every group is cleared, which ends the round.
diff: `groupStanding(game, g)` answers whether one specific group `g` has living monsters, and returns false for an out-of-range `g`. `roundGuard(ctx, game)` answers whether any group at all has living monsters, and takes no group index. For example, with group 0 empty and group 1 alive, `groupStanding(game, 0)` is false while `roundGuard` is true.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 6 decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, returning false if any character is not a digit or the string is empty or too long.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: For inputs of 1 to 6 characters, both return the same result. They diverge on inputs of 7 or more characters: A always returns false, while B returns true with the parsed value when it is at most 1000000. Examples: "1000000" (A false, B true with 1000000), "0000001" (A false, B true with 1), "0000000" (A false, B true with 0). Inputs of 7 or more characters with value above 1000000, such as "1000001", are false in both.

what_a: Collects the name of every monster definition in the loaded game data into a list of strings and returns it.
what_b: Returns a reference to the monster definition at the given index in the game data's monster list, with no game rules applied.
diff: Function A returns a vector of every monster's name, while Function B returns a reference to one MonsterDef selected by index. They have different return types and different purposes, so no input makes them give the same result.

what_a: Reads an integer field `k` from a JSON object `o`, returning it as an i32 or 0 if the key is missing.
what_b: Returns a monster's levelFound field cast to a 32-bit integer, standing in for a missing floor field in the monster data.
diff: Function A takes a JSON object and a key and returns the integer under that key, or 0 if the key is missing. Function B takes a MonsterDef and returns its levelFound field. They take different parameter types and read different data, so no input gives matching behaviour at a call site.

what_a: Converts a currency amount stored in 1/10000-gold units into its whole-gold part, formatted as text for display in the confinement (pens) shop screens.
what_b: Formats a gold amount stored in 1/10000 gold units as a decimal string with a " gold" suffix, omitting the fractional part when it is zero.
diff: Every input where the currency value is not a whole multiple of 10000 differs. For v=15000 (1.5 gold), A gives "1" and B gives "1.5 gold"; for v=5, A gives "0" and B gives "0.0005 gold". For whole-gold inputs such as v=20000, A gives "2" and B gives "2 gold", so they still differ unless confNumText itself appends " gold", which its body (not shown) would have to do. Negative inputs also differ, because B's digit extraction on a negative fraction produces non-digit characters.

what_a: Scans the pack inventory from slot 1 upward (skipping the Hands slot at 0) and returns the index of the first slot whose item id is 0, or -1 if the pack is full.
what_b: Refuses a pack slot of 1 (the hands, not an item) by setting the player-facing reply "Slot 1 is your hands, not an item." and returning false, otherwise accepting the slot.
diff: Not interchangeable for any input. A returns the index of the first empty pack slot (ItemId == 0) at or after index 1, or -1 if none; B returns false with a "Slot 1 is your hands" reply when the slot equals kFirstPackSlot and true otherwise. Only B has side effects (writing `reply`), and A never refuses slot 0.

what_a: Looks up a string value by key in the session's featureState map for the seer's pending person offer, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string-valued key in a JSON object and returns its string value, or an empty string if the key is missing.
diff: They take different containers (`Session::featureState` map vs. `JsonValue` object), so call sites can't swap without changing the object passed in. For a present key, A returns the stored `Str` unchanged, while B returns `v->asString()`, so any non-string JSON value (number, bool, null, object) yields whatever `asString()` produces, which I haven't inspected. For a missing key, both return an empty `Str`.

what_a: Maps a Race enum value to its display name string ("Human", "Elf", ..., "Troll"), returning "?" for unknown values.
what_b: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
diff: They take different enum types (Race vs Guild), so no argument is valid for both and they cannot be substituted at a call site. Their outputs are disjoint: raceName returns race names (Human, Elf, ... Troll) and guildName returns guild names (Nomad, Warrior, ... Healer). Both return "?" for an out-of-range value.

what_a: Looks up a race's base resistance to a given damage kind from the race table, returning 0 if the race or resistance entry is missing, as the first step of the game's resistance calculation.
what_b: Looks up a character's race in the race table and returns that race's size value, or 0 if the race index is out of range, which feeds the game's member-ordering logic.
diff: Not comparable at any input. A returns the race's damage-resistance value for a given `DamageKind` (`def.resistances[resistIndex(kind)]`), while B returns the race's `size` field and takes no damage kind. Both return 0 for an out-of-range race index, but that shared guard does not make them interchangeable.

what_a: Joins the words of a token list from a given index onward into a single string separated by spaces, used to rebuild a spell name or id from the typed command's remaining words.
what_b: Joins the words of a string vector from a given starting index into one space-separated string.
diff: They differ only when the words at the start of the range are empty strings. Function A puts a space before every word after `from`, while Function B only adds a space once its result is non-empty. Examples: `w={"", "x"}, from=0` gives A=" x" and B="x"; `w={"", "", "x"}, from=0` gives A="  x" and B="x"; `w={"",""}, from=0` gives A=" " and B="". Once a non-empty word has been added, the two match, as they do for any input with no empty words.

what_a: Returns a reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, by converting the coordinates to a cell index.
what_b: Returns a pointer to the square at 1-based coordinates (x, y) in a floor's row-major square array, or nullptr if the coordinates fall outside the 30-wide map or past the end of the stored squares.
diff: Out-of-range inputs differ: B returns nullptr for x < 1, y < 1, x > 30, or an index at or past squares.size(), while A computes cellOf(x, y) and indexes unchecked, which is undefined behaviour or a wrong square. Returning a non-const reference (A) versus a const pointer (B) also means call sites that check for nullptr can't take A without changing code beyond argument form. For in-range inputs the results match only if cellOf(x, y) equals (x - 1) + 30 * (y - 1), which I could not verify because cellOf's definition wasn't provided.

what_a: Builds the full set of six character attributes (STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, DEX) by taking each stat's value with all modifiers applied, such as race and equipment bonuses.
what_b: Maps a stat index (0–5) to its three-letter abbreviation (STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, or DEX as the fallback), which is text formatting for display.
diff: Not replaceable at any call site. A takes a Character and returns an array of kStatCount i32 values (each the modified stat). B takes an i32 index and returns a three-letter string label ("STR", "INT", "WIS", "CON", "CHA", or "DEX" for any other value, including out-of-range inputs).

what_a: Returns the height of a floor map by dividing its total field count by the floor's own width, or 0 if the width is non-positive.
what_b: Looks up the square at the given x, y coordinates on a dungeon floor, using the floor's width from the game data (or a default width), and returns a pointer to it or null if the level or coordinates are invalid.
diff: Not comparable at any input. mapHeight(def) returns an i32 height (fields.size() / def.width, or 0 when width <= 0). rescueSquareAt(s, level, x, y) returns a SquareState* to the square at (x, y) on a floor, or nullptr. One returns a number and the other returns a pointer, so no call site could swap one for the other.

what_a: Builds the full set of six character attributes (STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, DEX) by taking each stat's value with all modifiers applied, such as race and equipment bonuses.
what_b: Computes a character's base value for one attribute (STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, or DEX) from their race's minimum and maximum, starting at the race minimum plus the free per-stat points and capped at the race maximum.
diff: Not interchangeable at any call site. A takes a `Character` and returns the full array of modified stats via `statWithMods`. B takes a context, race, and stat index, and returns a base value `min(race.max[i], race.min[i] + 5)`. Their inputs, outputs, and purposes differ, so no input makes them substitutable.

what_a: Tests whether a given bit (0–31) is set in a 32-bit flags value, returning false for out-of-range bit indices.
what_b: Casts a signed 32-bit index to an unsigned 32-bit integer with no game meaning.
diff: They have different types and purposes. A takes a u32 flags word and an i32 bit index and returns a bool (false for bit < 0 or > 31, otherwise the bit's value). B takes an i32 and returns its u32 reinterpretation with no bounds check. For example, uidx(-1) returns 4294967295, while specialFlagBit(flags, -1) returns false, and specialFlagBit(0b100, 2) returns true where uidx(2) returns 2.

what_a: Copies named integer and string fields and one integer array from a parsed JSON object into a SpellDef record, a generated loader that maps spell-table data fields onto struct members.
what_b: Copies the "areaId" and "flags" integer fields from a parsed JSON object into a FloorField struct, with no game rules applied.
diff: Not comparable in the replacement sense. A fills a SpellDef from 15 keys (tableIndex, name, id, category, level, u4, killEffect, affectMonster, affectGroup, damage1, damage2, specialEffect, effect, required, resistIndex), while B fills a FloorField from 2 keys (areaId, flags). They target different types and read different fields, so they serve different purposes.

what_a: Returns a reference to the item's definition by indexing the game's item table directly with the item's id, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by converting the signed index to an unsigned value and indexing the party's member array, with no game rule applied.
diff: They index different containers and return different types: A returns a const `ItemDef&` from `ctx.data.items` keyed by `item.id`, while B returns a mutable `Character&` from `party.members` keyed by an `i32 index`. Neither can stand in for the other at any call site.

what_a: Computes the spell point cost a party member would pay to cast a given spell with no item involved, returning false if the member or spell doesn't exist.
what_b: Handles the player's typed "cast <member> <spell>" command in the dungeon, checking the caster and spell, applying the gate, reach and spell-point rules, and returning a message for the player.
diff: bufferSpellCost returns false when the member or spell is missing and otherwise returns the cost through `out`. dcastRun returns a reply string and always returns true. It refuses for bad usage, an unknown member or spell name, combat spells, unsupported effects, a failed gate, an unreachable spell, or insufficient SP, and it deducts SP after a successful effect. The one shared step is the same `castCostSp(..., 0)` call, so the computed cost matches wherever both reach it.

what_a: Returns the smaller of two 64-bit integers, a general math helper with no game meaning.
what_b: Returns 2 raised to the power k as a 64-bit integer by left-shifting 1, a math helper with no game meaning.
diff: Not the same rule: minI64(a, b) returns the smaller of two values, while pow2(k) returns 2^k as an i64 (1 shifted left by k). For example, minI64(3, 5) = 3, but pow2(3) = 8 and minI64 takes two arguments where pow2 takes one. Pow2 also has a documented limitation: it is exact only while the result fits in i64, unlike the BigInteger reference.

what_a: Converts a 1-based item alignment value (Good, Neutral, Evil) into a 0-based pen index by subtracting one.
what_b: Converts a 0-based pack index into a 1-based player slot number by adding one, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: For every input, Function A returns packIndex-independent value align−1 (e.g. Good→0, Neutral→1, Evil→2), while Function B returns packIndex+1 (e.g. 0→1, 1→2); they are not equivalent for any input range, and A takes an enum while B takes an i32, so they cannot be swapped at call sites.

what_a: Maps a ChestTrap enum value to a human-readable trap name string, falling back to "unknown" for unrecognized values.
what_b: Maps a Race enum value to its display name string ("Human", "Elf", ..., "Troll"), returning "?" for unknown values.
diff: They take different enum types (ChestTrap vs. Race) and return different sets of strings (trap descriptions such as "poison gas" and "slime" vs. race names such as "Human" and "Dwarf"), so no input is valid for both and neither can replace the other.

what_a: Handles the player's identify command for one pack slot of a party member, validating the member and slot, then reporting in the reply whether the item was identified, already fully identified, unaffordable, or empty, along with the fee.
what_b: Identifies an item for a fee: if the slot is empty or the item is already fully identified it reports that, otherwise it charges the payer the identify fee from their purse and sets the item's identification level to All.
diff: (1) Out-of-range input: A rejects a member index outside `[0, party.size)` or a slot outside `[kFirstPackSlot, kLastPackSlot]` with a "No such party member." or "No such pack slot." reply and changes nothing, while B has no bounds checks and would act on whatever `Character&`/`Item&` it is given. (2) Return value: A returns void and reports through the `reply` string, while B returns an `IdentifyOutcome` that the caller must handle. (3) Messages: A's reply text states the fee and the payer's name or slot, which B never produces. For valid inputs the state changes match (the same fee is charged, and `idLevel` is set to `All` only when the item is identified), so the difference is in interface and reporting, not in the rule applied.

what_a: Looks up a string value stored under a constructed "hall.<k>.<field>" key in the session's feature state, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string-valued key in a JSON object and returns its string value, or an empty string if the key is missing.
diff: Not replaceable at any call site. A looks up `hallKey(k, field)` in `s.featureState` and returns the stored string or an empty `Str`. B looks up key `k` in a JSON object and returns `asString()` of the value or an empty `Str`. They take different inputs (a Session plus an integer key and field name, versus a JsonValue plus a key), and they read from different sources.

what_a: Parses an optional 1-based group number from a command token at a given position, and returns it as a 0-based index clamped to the valid group range (defaulting to the first group when absent or invalid).
what_b: Returns the index of the first living monster in group `gi` of an encounter (the one with hits above zero), or -1 if the group index is invalid or no member is still alive.
diff: Not comparable at any input. groupIndex parses a 1-based group number from a token and returns a clamped 0-based index, while frontLiving takes a group index and returns the position of the first living monster in that group, or -1.

what_a: Returns the item's alignment field as a 32-bit integer, with no game logic applied.
what_b: Returns a monster's levelFound field cast to a 32-bit integer, standing in for a missing floor field in the monster data.
diff: Function A returns the item's `alignment` field, while Function B returns the monster's `levelFound` field; these are unrelated attributes of different types (Item vs. MonsterDef), so no argument form makes one a drop-in replacement for the other, and they differ for every input.

what_a: Converts a 32-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives and "0" for zero.
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold currency amount as a decimal gold string with a minus sign for negatives and four fractional digits zero-padded.
diff: Every input gives different output. A(v) is the plain decimal integer (A(0)="0", A(12)="12", A(-5)="-5"), while B(c) is fixed-point gold with a decimal point and four fractional digits (B(0)="0.0000", B(12)="0.0012", B(-5)="-0.0005", B(10000)="1.0000"). B also overflows (undefined behaviour) on c = INT64_MIN because `-c` cannot be represented, whereas A is safe for every i32 because it widens to i64 first.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based party member number and returns false if the text isn't a number or falls outside the valid party size range.
what_b: Parses a party member number from the second word of a typed command and checks that it falls within the current party size, returning whether it is valid.
diff: The upper bound differs. A accepts 1..kPartyMaxSize (a fixed constant), while B accepts 1..accPartySize(s) (the session's current party size). For example, with a party of 2 and kPartyMaxSize of 4, input "3" is accepted by A and rejected by B. Their inputs also differ: A takes the already-extracted text, while B takes a token vector and returns false when it has fewer than 2 entries. Parsing may differ too, since companionsParseNumber and accParseInt are not shown, so inputs such as "+2", " 2", or "2x" may be handled differently.

what_a: Returns the name of the party member at the given index in the session, or an empty string if no such member exists.
what_b: Looks up a stored record field (for a given kind and name, such as a monster or item entry) in the session's feature state and returns its string value, or an empty string if it is absent.
diff: Not applicable. Function A returns a Character's name looked up by member index through `accMember`, while Function B returns a string from `featureState` looked up by a composed record key (prefix, kind, name, field). They take different parameters and read different data, so no input makes them interchangeable.

what_a: Checks whether the typed text names a valid pack slot (2 through kPackSlots, since slot 1 is the Hands) for a give command and returns that slot number, or -1 to signal "No Item to give!".
what_b: Checks whether a typed swap slot is a valid pack slot, refusing slot 1 (the hands, which never move) and any slot beyond the pack's limit.
diff: Range rule is identical: for an in-range integer slot n, A accepts exactly when B does (2 <= n <= kPackSlots). They differ in form: A takes text, parses it with giveCLng, and returns the slot number or -1, so a non-numeric string gives -1 and a valid slot gives n rather than true. B takes an i32 and returns bool. Call sites would need changes beyond argument form, since the return type and sentinel differ. A's parse also accepts i64 inputs that B's i32 parameter cannot represent.

what_a: Handles the player's typed `buffer` command, listing a party member's spell buffers or setting or clearing one of their four buffer slots to a named spell, and returning the reply text.
what_b: Registers the "buffer" player command on the Town and Combat screens, so a player can set or list a member's spell buffers from either screen.
diff: Function A is a command handler that parses arguments and reads or mutates session state, while Function B is a void registration routine that only calls registerFeatureCommand twice (for Town and Combat screens) and never handles a command; no input to B produces a reply like A's, so there are no comparable inputs where results match or differ.

what_a: Reports whether a monster group in the current encounter is still standing, meaning it has at least one living member, and returns false for any out-of-range group index.
what_b: Returns the index of the first monster group that is currently standing, or -1 if no group is standing, ignoring the `delta` argument.
diff: Different return types and purposes. A returns `bool` (true iff the group index is in range and `livingCount > 0`), while B returns `i32` (the first standing group index, or -1 if none). A cannot replace B or the reverse. For example, A(game, 2) returns true when group 2 is standing, whereas B(ctx, game, d) returns 2 only if group 2 is the lowest-numbered standing group, and returns -1 when no group is standing. B's `ctx` and `delta` parameters are unused, and B is built on A's predicate.

what_a: Rolls a percentile die (one random draw) against a hit threshold, returning true if the attack passes the gate, per the Mordor melee hit rule R18 (miss when roll reaches the threshold).
what_b: Rolls a percentile die (1–100) against the monster's computed hit chance, returning true if the monster's attack hits the character.
diff: Both use a uniform roll in 1..100, but A passes when roll < threshold and B passes when roll <= chance. For integer values, A(threshold=t) matches B(chance=t-1) exactly, so they differ at every integer value: at 50, A passes 49 rolls (49%) and B passes 50 (50%). For fractional chance, no integer threshold reproduces B: at 5.4, B passes rolls 1-5 (five values), while A passes four at threshold 5 and five at threshold 6. Chance below 1 (e.g. 0.5) passes nothing in B, which matches A only at threshold 0 or lower. A also draws via ctx.rng.nextDouble() and B via ctx.rng.below(100), so even with identical distributions, the same seed may produce different outcomes (not verified from the code shown).

what_a: Parses a string of digits into a non-negative integer, rejecting empty strings, signs, non-digit characters, and values above 100000.
what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: Negative inputs: "-5" (and "-0", "-100000") are rejected by A but accepted by B (giving -5, 0, -100000). Values above 100000 up to 1000000000000: "100001" and "999999" are rejected by A but accepted by B. Values above 1000000000000 (e.g. "1000000000001") are rejected by both. A returns i32 and B returns i64, so B can represent results A cannot, though this only matters for inputs already listed. Empty input and "-" alone are rejected by both, and all inputs in 0..100000 give identical results.

what_a: Converts a 1-based item alignment value (Good, Neutral, Evil) into a 0-based pen index by subtracting one.
what_b: Converts a 1-based player slot number to a 0-based pack index by subtracting one, with no game rule applied beyond the slot numbering convention.
diff: none

what_a: Returns true while any encounter group still has living monsters, so the combat round continues, and returns false once every group is cleared, which ends the round.
what_b: Counts how many monsters in the current encounter are still alive, which the combat round logic uses to decide whether the fight continues.
diff: (1) Return type and value: A returns bool and B returns a count, so with 2 living foes A gives `true` and B gives `2`; with 0 both are falsy. (2) Data source: A reads each group's `livingCount`, while B counts monsters whose `alive` flag is set. Where those disagree, results differ. For example, a group with `livingCount == 1` and no monster flagged alive gives A `true` and B `0`. Monsters not covered by the first `kMaxGroups` groups are counted by B but ignored by A.

what_a: Copies the fields of a monster definition from a parsed JSON object into a MonsterDef struct, reading each stat, flag, and item list by name from the generated data file.
what_b: Copies the `spawnMask` and `lairId` integer fields from a parsed JSON object into a FloorArea struct, with no game rule applied beyond reading the values.
diff: They populate different types and different fields. Function A fills a MonsterDef (about 40 fields, including name, the arrays via getarr, and damageMod via getd). Function B fills a FloorArea with only spawnMask and lairId. Neither can stand in for the other at any call site.

what_a: Builds a new character's six base stats by taking each stat as the lower of the race's maximum and its minimum plus 5, using the rules' createBase calculation.
what_b: Returns the maximum value a character of the given race may reach for the given stat, which is the race's base stat maximum plus a fixed offset of 5.
diff: They compute different quantities for the same inputs. For a stat with race Min=10 and Max=18, A returns min(18, 10+5) = 15 while B returns 18+5 = 23. A returns a starting base value and B returns an upper bound. A also returns all six stats from a session, while B returns one stat and ignores its context argument. A's result depends on the createBase body, which was not shown, so this relies on its comment.

what_a: Returns the gold needed to advance from the membership's current level, calculated with that membership's guild gold factor (SRD R25).
what_b: Checks whether a character's guild membership can advance to the next level, returning false at the guild's maximum level and otherwise true only when the membership's experience meets the threshold from the level-up formula for its current level, race, and guild.
diff: Return types and purposes differ. goldForNextLevel returns the Currency cost to advance from the current level, while canLevelUp returns a bool saying whether the character may level up now. Every call site expecting one cannot take the other.

what_a: Checks whether a guild member's experience has reached the threshold required for the next level, returning true if so (R20.3).
what_b: Computes the experience cap for a character's current level in a guild, which is the XP threshold for the next level minus one, scaled by the guild and race experience factors.
diff: A returns a bool (experience >= xpRequired) and B returns an i64 (the XP threshold for level+1 minus 1), so no input makes them interchangeable and they cannot replace each other at call sites.

what_a: Checks whether a typed swap slot is a valid pack slot, refusing slot 1 (the hands, which never move) and any slot beyond the pack's limit.
what_b: Refuses a pack slot of 1 (the hands, not an item) by setting the player-facing reply "Slot 1 is your hands, not an item." and returning false, otherwise accepting the slot.
diff: Both refuse slot 1 (the hands). A also refuses slot 0, negative slots, and slots above kPackSlots (e.g. 41), where B accepts them. B returns a reply message on refusal and A does not. This assumes kFirstPackSlot is 1.

what_a: Returns true for the item types (23–28, 30, 31) that the original game removes from the pack once their last charge is spent, per MAINMOD2.BAS sub1149.
what_b: Reports whether an item kind is one of the combinable item types (kinds 23–28, 30, 31) that the original game allows the player to combine, mirroring the Select Case list in FRMCTYS.BAS.
diff: none

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, handling negative values and the minimum-value edge case by working with an unsigned magnitude.
diff: Only v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). A negates it with signed arithmetic, which overflows (undefined behaviour) and in practice yields "-". B uses unsigned magnitude and returns "-9223372036854775808". All other inputs give identical strings.

what_a: Returns the trap chance for a chest's treasure class (0 to 3), giving 0 for any out-of-range class, as set by the game's chest trap table.
what_b: Generates a fight-left chest on a square by rolling its treasure class, trap, magic lock, gold (scaled by group standing, lock and class), and chest items, storing the result on the chest.
diff: `trapChanceFor` takes a treasure class and returns an i32 trap chance (0 for classes outside 0..3, otherwise `kTrapChanceByClass[cls]`), with no side effects. `generateEncounterChest` is a void procedure that takes a chest, lead monster, and monster groups, then mutates the chest's trap, lock, gold, and items. It does not return a chance value, and it never calls `trapChanceFor`; it calls `rollChestTrap`.

what_a: Searches a list of floor states for the one whose dungeon level matches the given level and returns its index, or -1 if none matches.
what_b: Returns the index of the item definition in the data table whose id matches the given item's id, or -1 if none is found.
diff: They search different containers by different keys: A scans `floors` for `dungeonLevel == level` and takes an `i32` level, while B scans `ctx.data.items` for `id == it.id` and takes a `Ctx` and an `Item`. Neither can replace the other at any call site, since their argument types and element types differ.

what_a: Returns a reference to the item's definition by indexing the game's item table directly with the item's id, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by casting the signed index to unsigned and indexing the party's members array, with no game rule applied.
diff: Different purposes and types. A returns an `ItemDef` from `ctx.data.items`, looked up by `item.id` from an `Item`. B returns a `Character` from `party.members`, looked up by an `i32 index`. Neither can replace the other at any call site, whatever the argument form. Both also lack bounds checks, and B's signed-to-unsigned cast turns a negative index into a very large one.

what_a: Looks up a stored record field (for a given kind and name, such as a monster or item entry) in the session's feature state and returns its string value, or an empty string if it is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
diff: When the key is absent from `s.featureState`, A returns an empty string while B returns `dflt`, so they differ for any call where `dflt` is non-empty. A also builds its key as `kRecordPrefix + kind + "." + name + "." + field`, while B uses `key` verbatim, so they look up different entries for the same arguments. Results match only when `dflt` is empty and the key equals A's composed key. Found entries always return the stored value in both.

what_a: Rolls a quest for a guild member at the given guild level, returning none, a let-off, a defeat quest, or a fetch quest based on the SRD's quest percentages and level thresholds.
what_b: Assigns a guild quest to the player's membership by resetting the quest to an empty kind and recording only the guild level, since the quest kinds, targets and counts are not defined in the source text.
diff: Not comparable. Function A rolls for a quest outcome (kRollNone, kRollLetOff, kRollDefeat or kRollFetch) and returns it, consuming Rnd draws. Function B mutates the membership by setting an empty quest of kind None with the guild level recorded, and it returns nothing and draws no Rnd.

what_a: Applies the Gear A/D fit rule (R9) to a raw attack or defence value, returning it unchanged for a full fit, halved with round-half-to-even for a half fit, or negated for a subtract fit.
what_b: Given an item's alignment and a character's alignment, it returns how well the item fits the character (Full, Half, or Subtract): unaligned items always fit fully, and otherwise the fit depends on how far apart the two alignments sit on the Good-Neutral-Evil scale.
diff: They do different jobs with incompatible signatures. adWithFit(i32 raw, FitClass) returns an i32 value (raw, half-rounded, or negated), while fitFor(ItemAlign, Align) returns a FitClass, so no call site can swap one for the other.

what_a: Computes a character's effective resistance percentage against one damage kind by starting from the race's base value, replacing it with a fixed 90 if a counting item applies, and then taking the higher of that and the character's spell-raised resistance.
what_b: Returns the resistance value a creature gets from its gear, which is a flat 90 when the item grants resistance and otherwise the race's base resistance, with gear not stacking.
diff: Function A also applies the spell raise (`max(value, c.resistances.resist[...])`), which B never does. Whenever the spell value exceeds the gear-adjusted value, A returns the spell value and B does not. Examples: with no counting item and raceBase 20, a spell resist of 50 gives A = 50 and B = 20; with a counting item and a spell resist of 95, A = 95 and B = 90. Where the spell value is at or below the gear-adjusted value, the two agree.

what_a: Rolls a quest for a guild member at the given guild level, returning none, a let-off, a defeat quest, or a fetch quest based on the SRD's quest percentages and level thresholds.
what_b: Checks whether a character's current guild quest (none, defeat a monster, or fetch an item) is satisfied, and when asked to consume, removes the fetched item from the pack and increments the character's item-quest count.
diff: Not applicable. rollQuest (R43) rolls for a guild quest outcome and returns kRollNone, kRollLetOff, kRollDefeat, or kRollFetch, while questSatisfied (R45) checks whether an existing quest is complete and may consume a fetched item from the pack.

what_a: Maps a player's position and facing to the grid edge (wall, door, or secret door bits) they would cross when moving or looking in that direction, so that walls and doors can be checked against the dungeon floor data.
what_b: Classifies the edge of a dungeon square in a given facing as a wall, door, secret door, or open passage, with anything off the map treated as a wall.
diff: edgeRefOf returns an EdgeRef (cell coordinates plus wall, door, and secret bit masks) and never reads the floor, while classifyEdge returns an EdgeClass (Wall, Door, SecretDoor, or Open) by reading the floor's cell bits; for every input their return types and results differ, and classifyEdge calls edgeRefOf internally.

what_a: Returns the fixed usage string for the options command, listing its three argument forms (show all, set one option, or set a party member's option).
what_b: Handles the typed `options` command: with no argument it lists all options, a numeric first argument routes to the character-specific option handler, and anything else goes to the game-wide option handler.
diff: Function A returns a fixed usage string and never reads its inputs. Function B takes a session and word vector, and returns a listing, a character command, or a game command depending on the arguments. Every input gives a different kind of result.

what_a: Builds the string key "quest.<member>.<guild>" used to store an open-quest flag for a given member and guild in featureState.
what_b: Handles the typed "quest <member>" command by checking that a named party member belongs to the Nomad guild, then assigning them a guild quest if none is open and replying with the appropriate message.
diff: questsKey returns a storage key string ("quest.<member1>.<guild>") and has no side effects, while cmdQuest is a command handler that parses arguments, validates the member and guild, assigns a quest, sets the open flag, and returns a reply string. No input makes them produce the same result, and they have different signatures and return types.

what_a: Checks whether the typed text is a case-insensitive prefix of a person's name, which the seer uses to match a player's answer against the pending person offer.
what_b: Reports whether a seer (the person-offer feature) currently has a pending offer stored in the session's feature state, which the game uses to track an offer until the player answers it.
diff: Not applicable. Function A is a case-insensitive prefix test on two strings, and Function B checks whether a session has a non-empty pending-offer entry. They take different parameters, return results with different meanings, and no input produces the same result from both.

what_a: Scans the pack inventory from slot 1 upward (skipping the Hands slot at 0) and returns the index of the first slot whose item id is 0, or -1 if the pack is full.
what_b: Scans one member's pack for the first empty slot (id <= 0), copies the item in with its equipped flag cleared, and returns whether a slot was found.
diff: (1) Start index: A scans from slot 1 and never considers slot 0, while B scans from slot 0. If pack[0] is free and the others are full, A returns -1 and B places the item in slot 0. With an empty pack, A returns 1 and B uses 0. (2) Free test: A treats only id == 0 as empty, while B treats id <= 0 as empty. An item with a negative id is occupied for A and free for B. (3) Side effects: B writes the item into the slot and clears `equipped`, while A only returns an index and changes nothing. (4) Return value: A returns a slot index or -1, and B returns true or false.

what_a: Looks up an item's definition record from the game's item table by its id, returning a pointer to it or null when the id is negative or out of range.
what_b: Linear search through the game's item list that returns a pointer to the item definition whose id matches the given id, or null if none exists.
diff: They agree only when `data.items[i].id == i` for every index i. They differ when (1) `item.id < 0`: A returns nullptr, while B returns any item with a negative id, if one exists; (2) `item.id >= items.size()`: A returns nullptr, while B returns the item whose id matches if ids are not positional; (3) the id is in range but `items[id].id != id`: A returns the wrong item, while B returns the item that actually has that id, or nullptr if none does; (4) duplicate ids: B returns the first match, while A returns `items[id]`, which may not be the first match.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal text representation, handling the sign and the most negative value without using the C library.
diff: Only for v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). Function A negates it, which overflows (undefined behaviour in C++, and it stays negative in practice), so the loop never runs and it returns "-". Function B returns "-9223372036854775808". All other inputs, including 0, positive values, and every other negative value, produce identical strings.

what_a: Maps a ChestTrap enum value to a human-readable trap name string, falling back to "unknown" for unrecognized values.
what_b: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
diff: They take different enum types (ChestTrap vs. Guild) and return different content: A returns trap descriptions such as "poison gas" and "slime", while B returns guild names such as "Nomad" and "Warrior". No input yields the same purpose, and they cannot substitute for each other at any call site.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: They accept different inputs with length or magnitude above 4 digits. A rejects any input longer than 4 characters, so "10000", "12345", "1000000", and "00001" return false. B accepts those (values 10000, 12345, 1000000, and 1) because it only caps the numeric value at 1000000 inclusive, so "1000001" and larger are rejected by B and A alike. Both accept "9999" and reject "", "-5", and "12a". A's range is 0 to 9999; B's is 0 to 1000000.

what_a: Looks up a string value by key in the session's featureState map for the seer's pending person offer, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Clears the pending seer person offer (its kind, name, and level) from the session's feature state once the offer has been answered.
diff: Function A returns the value stored under `key` in `s.featureState`, or an empty `Str` if the key is absent. Function B returns nothing and erases the three keys `kSeerKindKey`, `kSeerNameKey`, and `kSeerLevelKey` from `s.featureState`. A never modifies the session and B never returns a value, so no call site could substitute one for the other.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its plain decimal string form, with a leading minus for negatives, without relying on the standard library's number formatting.
what_b: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal string representation, prefixing a minus sign for negatives, with no game meaning.
diff: Only for v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808). Function A negates it, the overflow leaves it negative, the digit loop never runs, and it returns "-". Function B negates it the same way, then recurses on the same value forever until the stack overflows. Both are undefined behaviour from signed overflow, so neither result is safe; for all other inputs, including 0 and every other negative and positive value, the two return identical strings.

what_a: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a non-negative integer, rejecting empty strings, signs, non-digit characters, and values above 100000.
diff: A accepts 100001 through 999999 (e.g. "100001", "999999") and B rejects them, since B caps values at 100000. B accepts zero-padded words longer than 6 characters (e.g. "0000001" gives 1), and A rejects them because of its length check of 6. Both accept "100000" and "0", and both reject "", "+5", "-5", and any non-digit.

what_a: Maps a player's position and facing to the grid edge (wall, door, or secret door bits) they would cross when moving or looking in that direction, so that walls and doors can be checked against the dungeon floor data.
what_b: When the party passes through a dungeon wall edge, it records that edge as a door (clearing any secret-door marker) and removes the wall marker, following the SRD c15p1 door-passage rule.
diff: Not comparable as replacements. edgeRefOf is a pure lookup that returns an EdgeRef (cell coordinates plus wall, door, and secret bit masks) for a cell and facing, and returns {x, y, 0, 0, 0} for an invalid facing. recordDoorPassage returns void and mutates floor.sqAt(e.cx, e.cy).bits, and it does nothing if the cell is out of range. recordDoorPassage calls edgeRefOf internally, so the two are layered rather than interchangeable.

what_a: Returns the display name of a monster's definition looked up by its index, or the fallback string "a monster" when no definition is found.
what_b: Returns a reference to the monster definition at the given index in the game data's monster list, with no game rules applied.
diff: Different inputs and outputs: A takes a Ctx and a Creature, resolves the index through monsterDefIndex, and returns a Str name; B takes a GameData and a raw index and returns a const MonsterDef&. For a valid index, A returns only the name and B returns the whole definition. For an invalid index (negative), A returns "a monster" while B casts to u32 and indexes out of bounds (undefined behaviour).

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based companion slot number, returning false if the text isn't a number or falls outside 1 to kCompanionSlots.
what_b: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
diff: Input "1" gives slot1 = 1 in A but idx = 0 in B. Every valid input differs by one because A returns 1-based and B returns 0-based. The upper bound also differs: A accepts 1..kCompanionSlots, while B accepts 1..s.game.party.size. A takes no Session, so its bound is fixed and does not depend on the party.

what_a: Parses a string of digits into an integer party slot number between 1 and kPartyMaxSize, returning -1 if the text is not a valid slot.
what_b: Parses a typed string as a whole number and reports whether it is a valid 1-based pack slot (1 to 39), storing it in the slot index.
diff: Interface: A returns the slot or -1, while B returns bool and writes the slot through an out-parameter. Range: A accepts 1..kPartyMaxSize, B accepts 1..39, so inputs such as "40" are rejected by B and accepted by A whenever kPartyMaxSize > 39. Input format: A rejects any string longer than 2 characters, so "007" is invalid for A and may be valid for B, depending on parseNum. A also rejects non-digits, so "+5" and " 5" are invalid for A, but B's parseNum may accept them. Empty input is rejected by A and depends on parseNum for B.

what_a: Converts an integer to its decimal string form, with no game meaning.
what_b: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, handling negative values and the minimum-value edge case by working with an unsigned magnitude.
diff: For every i32 input the two return identical strings, including 0 ("0"), negatives (-5 gives "-5"), and INT32_MIN ("-2147483648"). They differ only in input domain: B accepts any i64, but A takes i32, so an i64 outside [-2147483648, 2147483647] cannot be passed to A without truncation (e.g. 4294967296 becomes "0" through A after narrowing, versus "4294967296" from B).

what_a: Searches a list of library entries for one whose kind and name match the given values, ignoring name case, and copies the first match into the output parameter.
what_b: Returns the index of the first entry in a list of names that matches a given word, ignoring case, or -1 if none match.
diff: Not interchangeable for any input. A returns a bool and copies a matching LibEntry into `out`, matching on both `kind` and case-insensitive `name`. B returns the index (or -1) of the first match in a plain C-string array, matching only on name via `sameName`. Their return types and outputs differ, and A has no index or count parameters.

what_a: Checks whether the typed text is a case-insensitive prefix of a person's name, which the seer uses to match a player's answer against the pending person offer.
what_b: Clears the pending seer person offer (its kind, name, and level) from the session's feature state once the offer has been answered.
diff: Function A is a case-insensitive prefix test that returns a bool and does not modify the session, while Function B returns void and erases three pending-seer keys from `s.featureState`. They do not share inputs, outputs, or side effects, so no input produces matching results.

what_a: Looks up an item's definition record from the game's item table by its id, returning a pointer to it or null when the id is negative or out of range.
what_b: Returns a pointer to the spell definition at the given index in the session's spell data table, or nullptr if the index is out of range.
diff: Both perform the same bounds-checked index into a data table, but they read different tables and return different types: A returns `&ctx.data.items[id]` as `ItemDef*` and B returns `&s.data.spells[index]` as `SpellDef*`, so no call site can swap one for the other, even with a change of argument form. Any input gives different results: for example, index 3 yields an item in A and a spell in B.

what_a: Returns the `floor` field of the item at the given index in the game data's item list, converting the index to an unsigned integer for lookup.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by converting the signed index to an unsigned value and indexing the party's member array, with no game rule applied.
diff: Not replaceable at any call site. A returns an i32 copy of `items[idx].floor` from a const GameData. B returns a mutable Character reference from `party.members[index]`. The return types, the containers, and the purposes all differ.

what_a: Builds the string key "quest.<member>.<guild>" used to store an open-quest flag for a given member and guild in featureState.
what_b: Opens or closes a quest for a given party member and guild by setting or clearing that quest's flag in the session's feature state.
diff: For every input, A returns a string key ("quest.<member1>.<guild as int>") and does not touch the session, while B returns void and mutates `s.featureState` (sets "1" when open is true, erases the key when false). A cannot stand in for B or the reverse, and no argument-form change reconciles them.

what_a: Looks up a spell by name or id and returns its position in the session's spell table, so a spell buffer can store that index.
what_b: Handles the player's typed `buffer` command, listing a party member's spell buffers or setting or clearing one of their four buffer slots to a named spell, and returning the reply text.
diff: They do different jobs. A takes a spell name and returns a table index (or false if no spell matches), with no side effects. B parses a `buffer` command, writes or erases `s.featureState` entries, and sets a reply string. A is never a substitute for B, and B's behaviour (usage text, member and slot validation, the "clear" keyword, state changes) has no counterpart in A. A call such as `bufferFindSpell(s, "clear", idx)` can return false, while B treats "clear" as a keyword before any lookup.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal string representation, prefixing a minus sign for negatives, with no game meaning.
diff: Not interchangeable. glParseInt parses a string into an i64 and reports success through `ok`, while viewInt formats an i64 as a decimal string. Their signatures and purposes are inverse, so no call site could swap one for the other.

what_a: Decides whether a swing's aim must move to another target, returning true when the aimed group is invalid or no longer standing, per the melee rules (R2, R3, R5).
what_b: Implements R3 of the melee rules: further swings stay on the aimed group while it still has standing members, and otherwise aim shifts to the first standing group.
diff: Function A returns a `bool` (true when the aim must move), while function B returns an `i32` group index (the aimed group when it stays, otherwise a replacement group), so their return types and purposes differ for every input. B's fallback is `firstStandingGroup(enc)`, a stand-in for the unseen `fn0DCD(-1)` body, so B's behaviour in the move case is itself unverified.

what_a: Decides whether a dungeon square spawns an encounter, applying the game's rules for refusing rock and area 0, the lair roll, class and monster selection, and the target floor from the leader's level, then places the monsters on the square.
what_b: Decides whether a monster encounter can happen on the current square and area, returning Blocked (rock square, area 0, or zero spawn mask), UseStored (a stored encounter in a positive area), or Roll (proceed to the random encounter roll).
diff: Function A returns `bool` and mutates `s.game.encounter`, while Function B returns `EncounterPrecheck` (`Blocked`, `UseStored`, or `Roll`) and has no side effects. For any input where B returns `Roll`, A can still return false (for example, no party members, a missing floor definition, a zero-area square, or a failed lair or monster pick). A also checks `square.rockRecorded` and `hasEncounter || anyFoes` rather than B's `squareCode == kRockSquareId` and `hasStoredEncounter` alone, so a non-rock square with `rockRecorded` set is refused by A but not by B. A calls B and compares the result to `Roll`, so it is a caller of B, not an equivalent of it.

what_a: Checks whether the typed text names a valid pack slot (2 through kPackSlots, since slot 1 is the Hands) for a give command and returns that slot number, or -1 to signal "No Item to give!".
what_b: Returns the pack item at a given member and slot, or nullptr if the slot is the hands (slot 1), out of range, or empty (id ≤ 0).
diff: Different signatures and purposes. giveSlot takes a text string, parses it, and returns a slot number (2..kPackSlots) or -1. realignItemAt takes a Session, a member index, and a slot index, and returns an Item* (nullptr when the slot is empty or invalid). Their range checks also differ: giveSlot checks both bounds itself, while realignItemAt checks only the lower bound and relies on accPackItem for the upper bound. Input "1" gives -1 from giveSlot and nullptr from realignItemAt, and an in-range slot holding no item returns a slot number from giveSlot but nullptr from realignItemAt.

what_a: Copies the fields of a monster definition from a parsed JSON object into a MonsterDef struct, reading each stat, flag, and item list by name from the generated data file.
what_b: Copies the "areaId" and "flags" integer fields from a parsed JSON object into a FloorField struct, with no game rules applied.
diff: They populate different types (MonsterDef vs. FloorField) from different JSON keys. A reads ~35 monster fields (tableIndex, name, att, ..., kind); B reads only areaId and flags. No input yields the same result, and B cannot stand in for A or the reverse.

what_a: Returns a reference to the item's definition by indexing the game's item table directly with the item's id, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a reference to the monster definition at the given index in the game data's monster list, with no game rules applied.
diff: Not interchangeable for any input. A returns an `ItemDef` from `ctx.data.items`, indexed by `item.id`. B returns a `MonsterDef` from `data.monsters`, indexed by an `i32 lead`. Different tables, different return types, and different parameter types (`Ctx`+`Item` vs `GameData`+`i32`).

what_a: Takes the requested gold amount from the party's gold on hand, drawing from members in roster order, and returns false without taking anything if the party can't cover it.
what_b: Charges the gold fee for uncursing a character, drawing from gold on hand first and then the bank, and refuses without changing anything if the combined funds cannot cover it.
diff: A never touches bank gold and draws from the whole party in roster order, while B draws from one payer's hand first and then the bank. So when the amount exceeds the party's gold on hand but is covered by hand plus bank (e.g., hand 0, bank 100, amount 50), A returns false and B succeeds. When the party has enough gold on hand, A takes it from several members in roster order and B takes it from a single payer, so the per-member balances differ. With a negative amount, B adds to the payer's hand gold while A changes nothing.

what_a: Returns a reference to the inventory of the party member at the given index, converting the signed index to unsigned for container access; it has no game meaning of its own.
what_b: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index by casting the signed index to unsigned and indexing the party's members array, with no game rule applied.
diff: They return different types from different containers: A returns a non-const `Inventory&` from `p.inventories`, and B returns a `const Character&` from `party.members`. A takes a non-const `Party&` and B takes a `const Party&`. Both index unchecked with `static_cast<u32>(i)`, but that is the only shared behaviour, so no call site can swap one for the other.

what_a: Computes the damage of one melee swing in Mordor, combining level, strength, and damage modifier with a random roll and an attack-versus-defence adjustment, then applies the final hit gate that can turn the swing into a miss.
what_b: Returns true when a melee swing's damage is below 1, which the SRD rules R16 and R22 treat as a miss, so the attack deals no damage.
diff: Different signatures and return types. A takes (ctx, atk, def, level, strength, damMod), consumes RNG draws, and returns an i32 damage (0 on a miss). B takes an i32 damage and returns a pure bool. Neither can replace the other at a call site; the only overlap is that B's rule (damage < 1) applied to A's output matches A's miss outcome.

what_a: On entering a square, it rolls once for each not-yet-recorded secret door on the four edges touched, using the leader's ability value divided by a constant as the success chance, then records either the found door (clearing the wall) or the wall.
what_b: When the party passes through a dungeon wall edge, it records that edge as a door (clearing any secret-door marker) and removes the wall marker, following the SRD c15p1 door-passage rule.
diff: A is a probabilistic discovery roll on entry and B is a deterministic passage record, so they differ on every input where an edge has a secret bit: A with an unrecorded secret edge rolls and leaves it as a door (success, `ability/5 > roll`) or a wall (failure), while B always turns it into a door and clears the wall. Even with no roll, A never touches edges without a secret bit, while B clears the wall bit on any edge passed through and records a door bit where one exists.

what_a: Rolls a d100 for a chest and returns MAGIC_LOCKED if the roll is within the chance threshold, the chest class is above CONTAINER, and the square allows magic, otherwise UNLOCKED.
what_b: Decides whether a chest gets a magic lock by checking whether the square allows one, then rolls the lock chance against the chest's treasure class to return the resulting ChestLock.
diff: none. For any inputs, B returns exactly what A returns when A receives `squareAllowsMagicLock(squareBits)` as its bool, since B only computes that bool and forwards the remaining arguments. Both draw the die unconditionally, so the RNG stream matches.

what_a: Computes a guild's attack and defence ratings by adding the base attack/defence value (kBaseAD) to the best attack and defence values the guild has, per rule R12.
what_b: Builds the gear-screen summary line showing a character's combat attack/defence and total attack and defence, recomputed from the character and inventory each time.
diff: Function A returns an AdPair (`att = kBaseAD + best.att`, `def = kBaseAD + best.def`), while Function B returns a formatted display string ("Combat A/D …, total attack …, total defence …."), so no input gives the same result and they cannot be substituted at call sites.

what_a: Parses a string of digits into a 1-based party member number, returning 0 if the input is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string, returning the fallback value if the string is empty, contains a non-digit character, or exceeds 1,000,000.
diff: (1) Failure result: A always returns 0; B returns the caller's `fallback`, so they differ whenever fallback != 0 (e.g. `parseInt("", 5)` gives 5, `dcastParseMember("")` gives 0). (2) Magnitude: B rejects values above 1000000 (e.g. "1000001" gives fallback), while A accepts any value within its digit-count limit (e.g. "1000001" gives 1000001). (3) Length: A rejects words longer than `kMaxMemberDigits` even with small values (e.g. "0000001" if that limit is under 7); B has no length limit and accepts arbitrary leading zeros. (4) For very long digit strings A can overflow `i32` if `kMaxMemberDigits` is 10 or more, while B cannot overflow because of its 1000000 cap. Both reject empty strings, signs, and non-digit characters, and both return the parsed value otherwise.

what_a: Returns the absolute value of a 32-bit integer.
what_b: Returns the item's alignment field as a 32-bit integer, with no game logic applied.
diff: Function A returns the absolute value of its integer argument, while Function B takes an Item and returns its alignment cast to i32. They have different parameter types and different purposes, so they produce different results for every input.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based companion slot number, returning false if the text isn't a number or falls outside 1 to kCompanionSlots.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into an integer party slot number between 1 and kPartyMaxSize, returning -1 if the text is not a valid slot.
diff: Inputs with 3+ characters such as "001" or "010" are rejected by parseMember (returns -1) but may be accepted by companionsParseSlot, depending on companionsParseNumber, which isn't shown. Signed or padded text such as "+1" or " 1" is also a possible difference, since parseMember accepts digits only. If kCompanionSlots and kPartyMaxSize differ, valid upper bounds differ too. Return conventions differ: companionsParseSlot returns bool and writes slot1, while parseMember returns the slot or -1, so call sites need more than an argument-form change.

what_a: Returns the absolute value of a 32-bit integer.
what_b: Returns the number of entries in the monsters table of the game data, as a 32-bit integer.
diff: duseAbs(v) returns the absolute value of an integer argument and tableSize(ctx) returns the number of monsters in ctx.data; they take different inputs (an i32 versus a Ctx) and compute different things, so no input makes them interchangeable.

what_a: Returns true when an item is not yet fully identified (idLevel is not All), which is the condition under which the game charges an identify fee (rule R63).
what_b: Identifies an item for a fee: if the slot is empty or the item is already fully identified it reports that, otherwise it charges the payer the identify fee from their purse and sets the item's identification level to All.
diff: Every input differs in purpose and return type. A is a pure predicate returning `bool`. B is an action that returns `IdentifyOutcome`, mutates `item.idLevel`, and charges `payer`. For example, with an empty-slot item A returns true when idLevel != All, while B returns `EmptySlot`. With an unidentified, non-empty item that the payer can afford, A returns true and B returns `Identified` after setting idLevel to All and deducting the fee. With an item already at IdLevel::All, A returns false and B returns `NotNeeded`.

what_a: Sums the Def values of every equipped worn item in the inventory to give the character's total equipped defense bonus, which feeds into defenseOf.
what_b: Computes a character's Defense Adjustment (DefenseOf) as the base AD plus stat-based AD, the best guild AD defense bonus, and the sum of equipped item defense, floored at zero.
diff: `defenseOf` returns `max(0, baseAD + statsAD + best.def + equippedDef)`, while `equippedDef` returns only the raw sum of equipped item Def. They differ for every input where the other terms are nonzero (for example, any character with a nonzero base or stat AD, or with a guild AD bonus), and for any input where the total is negative, since `defenseOf` clamps to 0 and `equippedDef` does not.

what_a: Returns the facing direction a character would have after turning one step clockwise (right) from their current facing, wrapping North→East→South→West→North.
what_b: Converts a player's facing (N, E, S, or W) into the x and y step offsets used when moving one square in the dungeon, with north as +y and east as +x.
diff: Not interchangeable at any call site. A returns a Facing (the clockwise successor of f, assuming enum values N=0, E=1, S=2, W=3), while B returns no value and instead writes the (dx, dy) step for f through out-parameters. For every input, A's result is a direction and B's is a displacement, so no call site can swap one for the other.

what_a: Linear search over the game's floor list that returns a pointer to the floor whose dungeon level matches the given level, or null if none does.
what_b: Looks up the stored floor whose dungeon level matches the party's current dungeon level, returning nullptr if no such floor is saved.
diff: For any `level` equal to `s.game.party.dungeonLevel`, both return the same floor pointer (first match, or nullptr). They differ when `level` is any other value: A finds that floor, while B can only search the party's level. B also returns `const FloorState*` and takes `const Session&`, whereas A returns a mutable `FloorState*` and takes `Session&`, so A cannot replace B where a const pointer or const session is required, and B cannot replace A where mutation through the result is needed.

what_a: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
what_b: Maps each EquipProblem code to its fixed display string (such as "No Free Hands!"), returning an empty string for unrecognized codes.
diff: They take different enum types (Guild vs. EquipProblem), so no call site could pass the same argument to both. Their outputs also differ in kind: A returns a guild name ("Nomad", "Warrior", ...) and "?" on fallthrough, while B returns an equip error message and an empty string on default.

what_a: Decides whether a guild accepts a character of a given race by checking the guild's race bitmask, treating out-of-range race indices as allowed.
what_b: Looks up in the race-guild eligibility grid (T4) whether a given race is allowed to join a given guild, returning that yes/no answer.
diff: Both encode race-guild eligibility, but they read different data. A tests `guildDef.raceMask` bit `raceIndex`, while B looks up `kGuildGrid[raceIndex(race)][guild]`. A returns true for any negative index or any index >= kRaceRecordCount, whereas B has no such guard and indexes the grid out of bounds (undefined behaviour). For in-range inputs the results agree only if each guild's raceMask matches its grid column, which I could not verify from these two excerpts.

what_a: Attempts one step of party movement in the direction the party faces, refusing the move and reporting a wall hit when the step leaves the map, hits a wall or rock, and otherwise updating the party's position, door passage, arrival and lost-state records, and secret-door rolls per the dungeon exploration rules.
what_b: When the party passes through a dungeon wall edge, it records that edge as a door (clearing any secret-door marker) and removes the wall marker, following the SRD c15p1 door-passage rule.
diff: Every call site would change. A returns bool, refuses moves at map edges, walls, and rock, moves the party, runs arrival/lost handling, rolls secret doors, and calls B only for a successful Door or SecretDoor step. B returns void and only edits the edge bits of one square. For example, A on an open floor square moves the party and returns true, while B never touches party position; B on a wall edge rewrites door/wall bits where A returns false without recording a door.

what_a: Registers the "cast" dungeon-screen command, which lets a player cast a non-combat spell for a party member by name or id, with a usage hint shown in help.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "realign" command, which lets the player change an item's alignment for a fee, with its usage line shown to the player.
