diff: Different command names ("cast" vs "realign"), screens (Screen::Dungeon vs Screen::Town), handlers (&dcastRun vs &cmdRealign), and purposes (cast a non-combat spell vs change an item's alignment for a fee), and the argument forms differ too.

what_a: Reports whether a given party member has an open quest for a guild by checking the session's feature state for that quest key being set to "1".
what_b: Handles the typed "quest <member>" command by checking that a named party member belongs to the Nomad guild, then assigning them a guild quest if none is open and replying with the appropriate message.
diff: `questsHasOpen` is a pure read that returns whether the member's quest flag is "1". `cmdQuest` is a command handler that takes a `w` argument vector, can mutate the session (assigns a quest and sets the open flag), and writes a reply string. It always returns `true`, and its result depends on the input words and on the member's guild membership. The two cannot be substituted for each other at any call site, for any input.

what_a: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: B accepts a leading '-' and A rejects it (e.g. "-5" gives -5 in B, false in A; "-0" gives 0 in B, false in A). A accepts only 0 to 1000000 and B accepts 0 to 1000000000000, so "1000001" through "1000000000000" (and negatives in that range) succeed only in B. Both reject "", "-", "+5", non-digit text, and values above their own limits. Within A's accepted non-negative range the two agree, and A's output is i32 where B's is i64.

what_a: Looks up a companion's creature name from the monster table via its creature reference, falling back to "creature" when no definition is found.
what_b: Looks up a creature's monster-table index by its reference field, returning that index if it falls within the loaded monsters list and -1 otherwise.
diff: They return different kinds of value. A returns the monster's name string (or "creature" when the lookup fails). B returns the table index `m.ref` when it is in range, or -1 otherwise. Neither can stand in for the other at a call site.

what_a: Scans the game's floor table for the entry whose level number matches the requested level and returns a pointer to it, or null if none exists.
what_b: Scans the game's item table in order and returns the index of the first item whose type matches and whose floor is at least a given minimum, or -1 if none qualifies.
diff: They search different collections (`data.floors` vs `d.items`), match on different predicates (`levelNum == level` vs `Type == type && Floor >= low`), and return different things (`const FloorDef*` or `nullptr` vs an `i32` index or `-1`), so no input makes them agree.

what_a: Trims leading and trailing spaces and tabs from a string and returns the result, with no game meaning.
what_b: Splits a command string on spaces and tabs into a list of non-empty tokens, with no game meaning.
diff: Different return types and purposes. glTrim("  a b  ") returns the string "a b", while tokenize("  a b  ") returns the vector ["a", "b"]. glTrim("") and glTrim("   ") return "", while tokenize returns an empty vector. glTrim keeps interior spaces and tabs, but tokenize splits on them.

what_a: Returns a pointer to the spell definition at the given index in the session's spell data table, or nullptr if the index is out of range.
what_b: Looks up a spell in the game data by case-insensitive name first, then by numeric id if the text is all digits, returning a pointer to the matching spell definition or null.
diff: They take different inputs and answer different questions. A takes a spell-table index (an i32) and returns the element at that position, or nullptr if the index is out of range. B takes a text string, matches it case-insensitively against spell names, and falls back to matching a numeric spell id. For example, `bufferSpellDef(s, 0)` returns the first spell, while `castFindSpell(data, "0")` returns nothing unless some spell is named "0" or has id 0. Likewise `castFindSpell(data, "3")` returns the spell whose id is 3, which need not be `spells[3]`.

what_a: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal text representation, handling the sign and the most negative value without using the C library.
what_b: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, handling negative values and the minimum-value edge case by working with an unsigned magnitude.
diff: none. Both return the same string for every i64, including 0 ("0"), negative values (leading "-"), and INT64_MIN ("-9223372036854775808"). Both take the magnitude without overflow, and both emit digits in the same order.

what_a: Reports whether a given party member has an open quest for a guild by checking the session's feature state for that quest key being set to "1".
what_b: Rolls a quest for a guild member at the given guild level, returning none, a let-off, a defeat quest, or a fetch quest based on the SRD's quest percentages and level thresholds.
diff: Function A is a read-only lookup that returns true only when the quest's feature-state entry equals "1". Function B is a dice-roll engine that returns one of kRollNone, kRollLetOff, kRollDefeat, or kRollFetch, consuming RNG draws. Their return types and side effects do not match, so no input makes them interchangeable.

what_a: Compares two strings for equality ignoring case, returning true when the typed word matches the given name.
what_b: Returns the index of the first entry in a list of names that matches a given word, ignoring case, or -1 if none match.
diff: Not a replacement case. A returns a bool (case-insensitive equality of `word` and one `name`), while B returns an index: the first `i` in `[0, count)` where `sameName` holds, or -1 if none does. For example, `sameName("Sword", "sword")` is true, but `findIndex` with `{"sword"}` and count 1 returns 0, and with count 0 it returns -1 even when the name would match. B is built on A but does not do the same thing.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, handling negative values and zero without any game meaning.
what_b: Converts a signed 64-bit integer to its decimal string representation, prefixing a minus sign for negatives, with no game meaning.
diff: For v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808), A returns "-9223372036854775808", while B negates v, which overflows (undefined behaviour), leaves v negative, and recurses until the stack overflows. All other inputs, including 0, positive values, and other negatives, give identical strings.

what_a: Handles the player's typed "cast <member> <spell>" command in the dungeon, checking the caster and spell, applying the gate, reach and spell-point rules, and returning a message for the player.
what_b: Handles the player's typed combat commands (fight, defend, cast, use), validating each against the fight state and the caster's reach and spell points, then setting party orders and returning a reply message.
diff: A is an out-of-combat cast that applies its effect at once and spends SP afterward. B is an in-combat cast that queues an order and spends SP when the order resolves. A refuses Combat-use spells and B refuses NonCombat spells, so a Combat spell succeeds in B and fails in A, and a NonCombat spell does the reverse. A's refusal is about the spell's use; B's refusal is about being in a fight. B returns "You are not in combat" when no fight is active, where A proceeds. B refuses a dead member, which A does not check. A runs the unfit-gate check, which B does not. A takes all words after the member as the spell name, while B strips a trailing all-digit group number. An unknown spell name returns true in A and false in B.

what_a: Mapping (automap) is enabled for the party only when the leader is not lost, so a lost leader's party gets no map updates.
what_b: On arrival in a square, if the party leader is lost, the function ends the lost state when the square is already mapped, otherwise attempts to work out where the party is using the leader's perception, then shares the lost flags across the party.
diff: A returns `!leader.isLost()` as a bool and has no side effects. B is void and changes state: it returns early when the leader is not lost, but when the leader is lost it may call foundYourself and tryToWorkItOut and always calls shareLeaderLostFlags. For any party whose leader is not lost, A returns true and B does nothing. For any party whose leader is lost, A returns false while B runs its arrival logic. Their signatures also differ (A takes only the party; B takes ctx, floor, x, y as well).

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold currency amount as a decimal gold string with a minus sign for negatives and four fractional digits zero-padded.
diff: Every input except where the two formats coincide gives a different result. Examples: v=0 gives "0" (A) vs "0.0000" (B); v=5 gives "5" vs "0.0005"; v=-1 gives "-1" vs "-0.0001"; v=10000 gives "10000" vs "1.0000". B also depends on `viewInt`, which isn't shown, so its exact output for some inputs is unverified.

what_a: Attempts one step of party movement in the direction the party faces, refusing the move and reporting a wall hit when the step leaves the map, hits a wall or rock, and otherwise updating the party's position, door passage, arrival and lost-state records, and secret-door rolls per the dungeon exploration rules.
what_b: Maps an edge class (wall, door, secret door, or open) to its display name ("wall", "door", "secret door", "open") for the describe-square text, with "?" as a fallback for unknown values.
diff: Their signatures, return types, and purposes are unrelated. tryMoveForward takes a Ctx, Party, FloorState, and FloorDef, returns bool, and mutates party position, floor state, and automap records. edgeName takes an EdgeClass, returns the string name of that class, and has no side effects. No input makes them return the same result.

what_a: Rolls whether a treasure chest is trapped, based on its treasure class and the trap-flag bits, and if it is, picks which trap type applies.
what_b: Stores a chest's treasure class, trap, lock, and gold amount onto a square's record in the game's room state, marking the square as holding a chest only when the treasure class is positive.
diff: Not applicable. Function A computes and returns a ChestTrap (it rolls RNG, checks chance and trap flags, and can return NotTrapped), while Function B is void and only writes class, trap, lock and gold onto a SquareState. Neither can stand in for the other at any call site.

what_a: Decides whether a chest gets a magic lock by checking whether the square allows one, then rolls the lock chance against the chest's treasure class to return the resulting ChestLock.
what_b: Stores a chest's treasure class, trap, lock, and gold amount onto a square's record in the game's room state, marking the square as holding a chest only when the treasure class is positive.
diff: Not replaceable at any call site. A returns a ChestLock computed by rolling a lock (via rollChestLock) and mutates nothing. B returns void and writes class, trap, lock, and gold into the chest SquareState, deriving hasChest from treasureClass > 0. A takes a squareBits and lockedChance; B takes trap and gold and mutates the square.

what_a: Resolves the player's typed "seer yes" or "seer no" by either clearing the pending offer, or charging the fee and reporting the located character's position and whether they are alive.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "seer" command, which lets the player search for a creature, item, or person for a fee, and answer yes or no to a pending offer.
diff: Not comparable. seerAnswer handles a "seer yes"/"seer no" reply: it checks for a pending request, cancels on "no", or charges the fee, locates the character, and builds the reply. register_seer only calls registerFeatureCommand to register the "seer" command, with its town-screen binding and usage text, and returns void. Neither can stand in for the other at any call site.

what_a: Returns the spell point cost to cast a spell, which is zero when the cast comes from an item (itemLevel nonzero) and otherwise is the caster's spellbook cost from the spell cost engine.
what_b: Computes the spell-point cost of casting a given spell for the caster by checking each guild the caster belongs to that can reach the spell, pricing it with the guild's spell rate and the caster's guild spell level, and keeping the cheapest accepted price (raised to the smallest rated level seen), or 0 if no guild can cast it.
diff: For itemLevel == 0, A returns exactly what B returns, so B(ctx, caster, spell) is A(ctx, caster, spell, 0). For itemLevel != 0, A returns 0 while B returns its guild-based price, e.g. any caster with a qualifying guild and spell where B is nonzero.

what_a: Converts an uppercase ASCII letter to lowercase for the case-insensitive name matching the seer uses when checking whether a typed name starts with a given prefix.
what_b: Checks whether the typed text is a case-insensitive prefix of a person's name, which the seer uses to match a player's answer against the pending person offer.
diff: Not interchangeable. A maps one char to lowercase (A('Q') returns 'q', A('5') returns '5'). B takes two strings and returns a bool (B("Seer", "se") is true, B("Seer", "x") is false, B("Se", "seer") is false). B calls A internally, so they are related, but they do different jobs.

what_a: Converts a 1-based item alignment value (Good, Neutral, Evil) into a 0-based pen index by subtracting one.
what_b: Converts the player's typed word "good", "neutral", or "evil" (case-insensitive) into its item alignment code, returning -1 if the word is not recognised.
diff: Not interchangeable for any inputs. A takes an `ItemAlign` enum and returns `align - 1`, with no error case. B takes a string, lowercases it, and returns a code for "good", "neutral", or "evil", or -1 for anything else. A's input is an enum value and B's is text, so no argument-form change could make one stand in for the other.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits with an optional leading minus sign into a 32-bit integer, returning false if the text is malformed or the magnitude exceeds 1,000,000,000.
diff: A accepts magnitudes above 1000000000 and B rejects them, e.g. "1000000001", "-1000000001", "2147483647", "9999999999" (A returns ok=true with the value; B returns false). A accepts up to the i64 range (and overflows undefinedly past 19 digits), while B caps at ±1000000000 inclusive. On failure, A sets the return value to 0 and ok=false, while B returns false and leaves `out` unmodified. Both agree on "", "-", "+5", " 5", "12a" (reject) and "-0" and "1000000000" (accept, giving 0 and 1000000000).

what_a: Returns the pack item at a given member and slot, or nullptr if the slot is the hands (slot 1), out of range, or empty (id ≤ 0).
what_b: Scans one member's pack for the first empty slot (id <= 0), copies the item in with its equipped flag cleared, and returns whether a slot was found.
diff: Function A is a read-only lookup that returns a pointer to the item in a given (member, slot), or nullptr if the slot is below 2, out of range, or empty. Function B is a mutating search that writes the item into the first empty pack slot (id <= 0) and returns true, or returns false if the pack is full. They have different inputs, outputs, and side effects, so no call site could swap one for the other.

what_a: Converts a 1-based item alignment value (Good, Neutral, Evil) into a 0-based pen index by subtracting one.
what_b: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
diff: They do not share inputs or outputs. A takes an `ItemAlign` enum and returns `align - 1` with no validation or failure path. B takes a string, parses it, rejects non-numbers and values outside 1..party size, and returns a bool plus an out-parameter. The only overlap is the `-1` offset from 1-based to 0-based.

what_a: Looks up an item's definition record from the game's item table by its id, returning a pointer to it or null when the id is negative or out of range.
what_b: Looks up a spell in the game data by case-insensitive name first, then by numeric id if the text is all digits, returning a pointer to the matching spell definition or null.
diff: They search different tables with different keys. A looks up `ctx.data.items` by the integer `item.id` used as an array index (negative or out-of-range returns nullptr). B looks up `data.spells` by text: a case-insensitive name match first, then, for digit-only strings up to 9 characters, a scan for a spell whose `id` field equals that number, which is not an array index. Inputs where they diverge include: any item id (A returns an item; B has no items to search), an empty or blank string (B returns nullptr), and the string "5" (B searches for a spell with `id == 5` or a spell named "5", while A would return `items[5]`).

what_a: Builds the INI config key string "option.char<member>.<name>" for a character-option checkbox, using the member index as a digit and the name as the key suffix.
what_b: Handles the player's typed `char` command for the options screen, either reporting a party member's character option state or setting it on or off after validating the member number, option name, and on/off value.
diff: charKey(1, "Ambush") returns the storage key "option.char1.Ambush", while charCommand(s, {"opt","1","Ambush","on"}) returns the message "member 1 Ambush set to on." and writes "1" into s.featureState. charCommand also validates input and returns usage or error text, which charKey never does.

what_a: Looks up the square at the given x, y coordinates on a dungeon floor, using the floor's width from the game data (or a default width), and returns a pointer to it or null if the level or coordinates are invalid.
what_b: Checks whether a given square on a dungeon floor (1-based x, y coordinates) has a specific flag set, returning false for out-of-bounds coordinates.
diff: They return different types and answer different questions: A returns a mutable `SquareState*` (or nullptr), while B returns a `bool` that says whether a flag is set. Even as a pointer-or-null, A is not a substitute for B's boolean. Where both return "absent," they still differ: A returns nullptr when `level < 1`, when no floor matches the level, or when the index is outside the squares vector, while B returns false for those cases and also for `width <= 0`, `x < 1`, `y < 1`, or `x > width`. For x values outside 1..width, A's index can still land inside the vector and return a square from a neighbouring row, while B rejects them. A also falls back to `kRescueDefaultWidth` when the level is missing from `s.data.floors`, whereas B uses the width it is given.

what_a: Returns the treasure-class bonus added to a chest roll, granting it only when the chest comes from a lair and the second box-chance value is positive.
what_b: Rolls a random treasure class for a chest based on the lead monster's box chances, adjusted by a lair bonus that is currently always zero because the lair field is unknown.
diff: Function A returns the lair bonus (`kLairTreasureBonus` or 0), while Function B returns a treasure class from `classFromThresholds`. For any inputs, A's return value is an i32 bonus and B's is a class, so they cannot substitute for each other. B also hardcodes `lair = false`, so its internal call to A always yields 0.

what_a: Classifies the edge of a dungeon square in a given facing as a wall, door, secret door, or open passage, with anything off the map treated as a wall.
what_b: On entering a square, it rolls once for each not-yet-recorded secret door on the four edges touched, using the leader's ability value divided by a constant as the success chance, then records either the found door (clearing the wall) or the wall.
diff: Function A is a pure, read-only classifier that returns an EdgeClass, while Function B returns void and mutates the floor (clears the secret bit, sets the door or wall bit) and consumes RNG rolls. No call site could swap one for the other, and they agree on no inputs in the sense of producing the same result type or effect.

what_a: Checks whether a pack slot is a valid item slot (2 through kPackSlots, since slot 1 is the hands), which gates whether an item in that slot can be uncursed.
what_b: Scans the pack inventory from slot 1 upward (skipping the Hands slot at 0) and returns the index of the first slot whose item id is 0, or -1 if the pack is full.
diff: A is a bool predicate on a 1-based slot number (true for slots 2..kPackSlots, false for slot 1 and anything outside that). B returns an internal 0-based index of the first free pack entry (ItemId == 0) scanning indexes 1..kPackSlots-1, or -1 if none is free. A never looks at inventory contents, and B never returns a bool. The only overlap is the range: internal index i corresponds to slot i+1, so B's scan covers the slots A accepts.

what_a: Parses a party member number from the second word of a typed command and checks that it falls within the current party size, returning whether it is valid.
what_b: Checks whether a party member number entered for a typed swap falls within the valid 1-to-kPartyMaxSize range of party slots.
diff: Upper bound differs. A accepts members 1..accPartySize(s) and B accepts 1..kPartyMaxSize, so for a party of size 2 with kPartyMaxSize 6, member 3 gives A=false and B=true. A also rejects a missing or non-integer `words[1]`, which B has no equivalent for because it takes an already-parsed `i32`. B's 1-based numbering is an unverified assumption, so the lower bound matches A only if that assumption holds.

what_a: Reads a numeric field from a JSON object by key, returning its value as a double or 0.0 if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string-valued key in a JSON object and returns its string value, or an empty string if the key is missing.
diff: Return types differ (double vs Str), so no call site can swap one for the other. When the key is missing, A returns 0.0 and B returns an empty string. When the key is present, A calls asDouble() and B calls asString(). For example, getd on {"hp": 5} yields 5.0, while gets on the same object with "hp" yields "5" only if asString() converts numbers, and otherwise yields a conversion result that depends on the JsonValue type.

what_a: Opens or closes a quest for a given party member and guild by setting or clearing that quest's flag in the session's feature state.
what_b: Rolls a quest for a guild member at the given guild level, returning none, a let-off, a defeat quest, or a fetch quest based on the SRD's quest percentages and level thresholds.
diff: Not comparable. Function A stores or erases a feature-state flag in the session and returns void. Function B rolls a quest outcome, consumes RNG draws, and returns one of kRollNone, kRollLetOff, kRollDefeat, or kRollFetch. No call site could substitute one for the other, even with argument changes.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives.
what_b: Formats a 64-bit integer as a decimal string, with no game meaning.
diff: For v = INT64_MIN (-9223372036854775808), A negates v, which overflows (undefined behaviour in C++). In typical builds it wraps, the digit loop never runs, and A returns "-", whereas B returns "-9223372036854775808". All other inputs match.

what_a: Resolves the player's typed "seer yes" or "seer no" by either clearing the pending offer, or charging the fee and reporting the located character's position and whether they are alive.
what_b: Parses the player's typed "seer" command, showing usage help, answering the Seer's pending offer with yes or no, or dispatching a paid search for a creature, item, or person.
diff: seerCommand can't replace seerAnswer. seerCommand({"seer"}) returns the help text, while seerAnswer(s, true, reply) with nothing pending returns "Nothing is awaiting your answer." seerCommand({"seer","creature","x"}) starts a search, which seerAnswer never does. seerCommand({"seer","yes"}) matches seerAnswer(s, true, reply) only in the subset where it forwards to seerAnswer. Its input is also a word vector rather than a bool, and it lowercases the subcommand before dispatching.

what_a: Converts a 64-bit signed integer to its decimal text string, handling zero and negative values, with no game meaning.
what_b: Converts a 32-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives and "0" for zero.
diff: For every value in i32 range, including INT_MIN (-2147483648), both return identical text ("0", "-" + digits, or plain digits). A takes i64, so it accepts values outside i32 range (e.g. 2147483648), which B cannot represent without narrowing; narrowing those would change the output. For i64 INT64_MIN, A recurses forever (its `-v` overflows and stays negative), so it is undefined behaviour and a crash, while B is never given that value.

what_a: Tests whether a monster has a given special property bit set (the "Has(bit n)" check from rule R15 of the Mordor melee rules), returning true or false.
what_b: Tests whether a given bit (0–31) is set in a 32-bit flags value, returning false for out-of-range bit indices.
diff: none

what_a: Linear search over the loaded floor definitions that returns a pointer to the floor whose levelNum matches the given dungeon level, or null if none does.
what_b: Scans the game's floor table for the entry whose level number matches the requested level and returns a pointer to it, or null if none exists.
diff: Only when `data.floors.size()` exceeds 2^32-1. Function A's `u32` index wraps, so matches at positions >= 2^32 are never checked and it returns nullptr where B returns a pointer. This requires billions of floor entries, so it is unreachable in practice.

what_a: Returns a pointer to the spell definition at the given index in the session's spell data table, or nullptr if the index is out of range.
what_b: Looks up an item definition by its numeric id, returning a pointer into the item table or null when the id is zero, negative, or out of range.
diff: Index 0: bufferSpellDef(s, 0) returns &s.data.spells[0] when the spell table is non-empty, but defOf(ctx, 0) returns nullptr. The functions also read different tables (spells vs. items), so a call site would fetch different data even for the same index. Negative indices and indices at or past the end of the table are handled identically (nullptr).

what_a: Recalculates a character's maximum spell points from their abilities, then either fully restores current spell points on refill or caps current spell points at the new maximum.
what_b: Spell points gained from a Scroll of Spells or Tome of Spells are added to the character's current spell points and capped at their maximum.
diff: Function A recomputes `maxSpellPoints` from abilities and then either sets current to that max (refill) or clamps current down to it; it never adds points. Function B adds `amount` to current points and caps at the existing max, leaving max untouched. For example, with current=3, max=10, amount=4: A(refill=false) leaves current at 3, while B gives 7. A(refill=true) sets current to 10 regardless of any amount, while B has no refill mode. A also changes max when abilities differ, and B never does.

what_a: Case-insensitively matches a typed word against the quest guild names and, on a hit, sets the guild output to the matching enum value and returns true, otherwise returning false.
what_b: Parses a typed word as either a numeric index or a case-insensitive name into a Guild enum value, returning false if neither matches a valid guild.
diff: (1) Numeric input: B accepts a string that parses as an integer in 0..kGuildCount-1 (e.g. "2") and returns that guild, while A returns false. (2) Name table: A matches against kQuestGuildNames and B against kGuildNames, so any name present in one table but not the other is accepted by only one function. (3) Normalization: A applies accLower to both sides, while B lowers only the input and compares it to the raw kGuildNames entries, so an input differing only in accents or case can match in A but not B (or the reverse, depending on how accLower and lowered treat accents).

what_a: Rests every party member in town (dead ones included) by aging each by days computed from their hit-point loss, restoring their hits, and reporting the result, then if the first member aged, restocks the town store and pens by those days.
what_b: Computes the days a character spends resting in town from their missing hit-point percentage, then applies that aging to the character, returning the number of days.
diff: Not interchangeable at any call site. doRest takes (Ctx, Session, Str&) and rests the whole party, appending a note per member. restInCity takes (Ctx, Character&), ages one character, and returns the day count. doRest calls restInCity for each member, then replenishes the store and restocks the pens only when the first member aged (firstMemberDays > 0), which restInCity never does. Substituting restInCity for doRest would drop the party loop, the notes, and the town turnover, and substituting doRest for restInCity would require a Session and a reply buffer that restInCity does not take.

what_a: Maps a group's hostility state (hostile, engaged, or peaceful) to the word shown to the player in the fight description.
what_b: Implements the R18 group-hostility check, deciding whether a monster group's lead is engaged (hostile) toward the viewing party: a Good lead facing a Good viewer is peaceful, a Neutral lead is engaged with a 60% chance by rolling against a peace percentage, and an Evil lead (not yet specified) defaults to engaged.
diff: Not comparable. Function A maps a GroupState enum to a display string ("hostile", "engaged", "peaceful", or "?"), while Function B takes an alignment value and viewer alignment and returns a bool from a random roll, so no call site could use one in place of the other.

what_a: Returns the index of the first item in the item definition table whose type matches the given kind, or -1 if none does.
what_b: Linear search through the game's item list that returns a pointer to the item definition whose id matches the given id, or null if none exists.
diff: A matches on `it.type` (compared as `i32`) and returns an index or -1. B matches on `d.id` and returns a pointer or nullptr. Any call site that relied on one would get a different field searched and a different return form from the other.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
diff: Negative input: "-5" gives ok=true, value -5 in A, but false in B. Length: "12345" and "00001" give ok=true in A but false in B (B accepts at most 4 characters). Failure output: on failure A returns 0 and sets ok=false, while B leaves `out` unchanged. Overflow: A has no bounds check and overflows i64 on very long digit strings, while B cannot overflow. Both reject "", "-", and "+5" (A never accepts a leading '+').

what_a: Handles the player's typed "uncurse <member> <slot>" command by checking the slot's curse and equipped state, verifying the item's price and the member's gold, then clearing the slot's curse flag and charging the fee, or replying with the matching message.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "uncurse <member> <slot>" command, which lets a player pay a fee to remove a curse from an equipped item, and it is wired to the command handler cmdUncurse.
diff: Function A is the command handler: it takes a session, arguments, and a reply, validates input, checks the curse and equipped flags, charges the fee, and clears the slot curse flag. Function B takes no arguments, returns void, and only registers the "uncurse" command (town screen, handler pointer to A, usage string). B performs no uncurse logic, so the two cannot substitute for each other at any call site.

what_a: Looks up the character's best guild rating (attack and defence values) and returns them as an (att, def) pair, which the combat and total-AD rules use as input.
what_b: Computes a character's best guild attack and defense bonuses by taking the maximum att and def values across all guilds the character has joined.
diff: The only difference is the return type: bestGuildPair returns AdPair and bestGuildAD returns BestAd. For every Character, the att and def values are identical, because bestGuildPair just copies bestGuildAD's fields. Swapping them at call sites therefore needs changes to how the result is used, not just to the arguments.

what_a: Reads an integer field for a pending raise (resurrection) from the session's feature state by member and field name, returning the fallback value if the key is missing or the stored text doesn't parse as an integer.
what_b: Clears the pending raise state for a party member by erasing the stored chance, kind, and caster entries from the session's feature state, which ends a resurrection attempt in the game.
diff: A reads and returns an i32 (or the fallback), without modifying the session. B returns nothing and erases the "chance", "kind", and "by" entries for the member from featureState. No input makes them equivalent: they have different return types and opposite effects on state.

what_a: Looks up a spell by name or id and returns its position in the session's spell table, so a spell buffer can store that index.
what_b: Builds the text shown for a spell-buffer slot in a party member's pack, showing the spell or item name and its cost, or "(Nothing)" when empty, and clears the slot's stored buffer when the item it refers to no longer exists.
diff: Not comparable at a call site. A takes a spell name, looks it up with accSpellByName, and returns a bool plus the table index. B takes a member and slot, reads the buffer, and returns a display string, with side effects (erasing buffer state) and item and cost handling that A never touches.

what_a: Linear search over the loaded floor definitions that returns a pointer to the floor whose levelNum matches the given dungeon level, or null if none does.
what_b: Scans the game data's item list for the entry whose id matches the given id and returns a pointer to it, or null if none matches.
diff: They search different containers by different keys and return different types. A searches `data.floors` for `levelNum == dungeonLevel` and returns `const FloorDef*`. B searches `data.items` for `id == id` and returns `const ItemDef*`. For the same integer argument, they generally return different elements or nullptr, and the return types are incompatible, so call sites would not compile after substitution.

what_a: Returns a reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, by converting the coordinates to a cell index.
what_b: Looks up the square at the given x, y coordinates on a dungeon floor, using the floor's width from the game data (or a default width), and returns a pointer to it or null if the level or coordinates are invalid.
diff: For in-range coordinates on a floor whose width matches what `cellOf` uses, both return the same square. They differ when: (a) x or y is out of range, where B returns nullptr but A indexes out of bounds (undefined behaviour); (b) level < 1 or no floor has that dungeonLevel, where B returns nullptr and A has no such check; (c) the floor's width differs from the one `cellOf` uses, where the results differ, though `cellOf` is not shown, so this is unverified; (d) A returns a reference and B a pointer, so call sites need adjusting.

what_a: Copies the party leader's lost-state flags (level, position, facing, and whether lost) to every other party member and to the party-level mirror fields, so the whole party shares one lost status.
what_b: Mapping (automap) is enabled for the party only when the leader is not lost, so a lost leader's party gets no map updates.
diff: A is a void mutator that copies the leader's lost state to all members and sets `party.lostLevel`, `party.lostPosition`, `party.lostFacing`, and `party.lost = leader.isLost()`. B is a pure bool predicate returning `!leader.isLost()` and mutates nothing. A has no return value, so it cannot stand in for B at any call site, and B cannot perform A's side effects. The only shared element is the `leader.isLost()` check, which appears with opposite sign in each.

what_a: Computes the experience cap for a character's current level in a guild, which is the XP threshold for the next level minus one, scaled by the guild and race experience factors.
what_b: Computes the race experience multiplier f = (ln(r)/ln(r+1)) + 1 - 0.7 + r/25 from the race's experience factor plus one, using the SRD Chapter 5 formula for scaling experience by race.
diff: Not comparable. Function A returns an experience cap (an i64) from a character's guild level, guild and race factors, and a threshold lookup. Function B returns a race experience multiplier (a double) from one scalar, with no character, guild, or context input.

what_a: Cleans the guild log on the player's request by archiving all but the newest kGuildLogKeepOnClean entries to guildlog.text and keeping only those, provided the log has passed its cleaning threshold.
what_b: Registers the "guildlog" town command, which shows a chosen guild's log or cleans it down to the newest 50 entries.
diff: Function A cleans the guild log: if the log is over threshold, it archives all but the newest kGuildLogKeepOnClean (50) entries to guildlog.text and rewrites the log with those 50. Function B only registers the "guildlog" command with the Town screen and help text; it removes no entries and returns nothing. Their inputs and outputs do not correspond, so no input yields matching results.

what_a: Handles the player's "inspect" command at a chest by reporting whether a chest is present, whether it is trapped, and naming the trap if so.
what_b: Advances a chest's trap countdown by one step each tick and reports true once it drops below zero, meaning the chest opens, when a chest is present.
diff: Function A is a read-only query that reports whether a chest is trapped and, if so, its trap name, and it never changes state. Function B is a mutating timer that decrements `chestCount` and returns whether the chest opens. They return different types of result for every input, so no call site could substitute one for the other.

what_a: Converts a currency amount stored in 1/10000-gold units into its whole-gold part, formatted as text for display in the confinement (pens) shop screens.
what_b: Formats a signed Currency amount (1/10000 gold units) as a decimal gold string with trailing zeros trimmed and a " gold" suffix.
diff: For any v with v % 10000 != 0, A drops the fraction and B shows it: v=15000 gives A confNumText(1) and B "1.5 gold". For v=10000, A gives confNumText(1) and B gives "1 gold". For negatives, A truncates toward zero and B keeps the sign on the fraction: v=-15000 gives A confNumText(-1) and B "-1.5 gold". B always appends " gold", while A appends nothing unless confNumText does.

what_a: Looks up a string value stored under a constructed "hall.<k>.<field>" key in the session's feature state, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Reads a numeric field from a JSON object by key, returning its value as a double or 0.0 if the key is absent.
diff: Different return types and purposes: A returns a `Str` looked up from `s.featureState` by a hall key, while B returns a `double` read from a JSON object by key. A missing key gives an empty `Str` in A and `0.0` in B. Their results can't match for any input. B's result for a present but non-numeric JSON value depends on `asDouble`, which isn't shown.

what_a: Computes a character's base value for one attribute (STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, or DEX) from their race's minimum and maximum, starting at the race minimum plus the free per-stat points and capped at the race maximum.
what_b: Maps a stat index (0–5) to its three-letter abbreviation (STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, or DEX as the fallback), which is text formatting for display.
diff: Different purposes and return types: createBase returns an i32 base stat computed as min(race.max[i], race.min[i] + 5), while statAbbrev returns a three-letter Str label for index k (0 to 4 give STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, and any other value gives DEX). No input makes one a substitute for the other.

what_a: Returns the race definition for the given character race by indexing into the loaded race table, which supplies that race's stat minimums, maximums, and bonus points used in character creation.
what_b: Decides whether a guild accepts a character of a given race by checking the guild's race bitmask, treating out-of-range race indices as allowed.
diff: Different purposes and return types. Function A returns a `const RaceDef&` looked up by `static_cast<u32>(race)` with no bounds check, so an out-of-range `race` is undefined behaviour. Function B returns a `bool` saying whether a guild's race mask allows `raceIndex`: it returns true for any negative index or any index at or above `kRaceRecordCount`, and otherwise tests bit `raceIndex` of `guildDef.raceMask`.

what_a: Computes a character's StatsAD, the stat-based part of their armour/defence value, by summing weighted contributions from STR, DEX, INT and WIS through banded terms (rule R14), while ignoring CON and CHA.
what_b: Maps a stat index (0–5) to its three-letter abbreviation (STR, INT, WIS, CON, CHA, or DEX as the fallback), which is text formatting for display.
diff: Not comparable. statsAD takes a stat array and returns the i32 sum of weighted term() values over the bands for STR, DEX, INT, and WIS. statAbbrev takes an i32 index and returns a three-letter stat name string, with out-of-range values (including 5) mapping to "DEX". They share no inputs, outputs, or rule.

what_a: Joins the words of a token list from a given index onward into a single string separated by spaces, used to rebuild a spell name or id from the typed command's remaining words.
what_b: Joins the words of a string vector from index `from` up to `to` (clamped to the vector's size) into a single space-separated string.
diff: (1) Range end: A always runs to `w.size()`, so it matches B only when B's `to` is at least `w.size()`; for `to < w.size()`, B truncates and A does not. (2) Leading empty words: with `w = {"", "x"}, from = 0`, A returns `" x"` and B returns `"x"`; with `w = {"", "", "x"}, from = 0`, A returns `"  x"` and B returns `"x"`. B tests `out.empty()` rather than `i > from`, so it omits separators while the output is still empty. Both are the same for `from >= w.size()` (empty result) and for words with no leading empty strings.

what_a: Reports whether a seer (the person-offer feature) currently has a pending offer stored in the session's feature state, which the game uses to track an offer until the player answers it.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's featureState map for the seer's pending person offer, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
diff: Return types differ (bool vs. Str), so neither can replace the other at a call site. A is a predicate on one fixed key, while B is a getter for any key. A(s) equals `!seerGet(s, kSeerKindKey).empty()` for every session s.

what_a: Builds a namespaced string key ("raise.<member>.<field>") from a party member number and a field name, with no game meaning of its own.
what_b: Reads an integer field for a pending raise (resurrection) from the session's feature state by member and field name, returning the fallback value if the key is missing or the stored text doesn't parse as an integer.
diff: Not interchangeable at any call site. A returns a `Str` key (`"raise.<member>.<field>"`), while B returns an `i32` read from `s.featureState` (or `fallback`). B calls A internally to build its lookup key.

what_a: Returns a read-only reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, converting the coordinates to a flat index via cellOf.
what_b: Checks whether a given square on a dungeon floor (1-based x, y coordinates) has a specific flag set, returning false for out-of-bounds coordinates.
diff: Return types differ: A returns a `const SquareState&`, while B returns a `bool`, so no call site could substitute one for the other. Inputs also differ: A takes a `FloorState` and two coordinates, while B takes a `FloorDef`, two coordinates, and a `FloorFlag`. A does no bounds checking and B returns false for out-of-range coordinates. A's index comes from `cellOf`, which isn't shown, while B computes `(y-1)*width + (x-1)` itself.

what_a: Returns the race definition for the given character race by indexing into the loaded race table, which supplies that race's stat minimums, maximums, and bonus points used in character creation.
what_b: Returns a race's experience factor from the race table, which the game uses as a multiplier when computing experience gains for characters of that race.
diff: Return type differs: A returns a `const RaceDef&` (the whole race record), while B returns a `double` (only the `expFactor` field, converted). No input makes them agree in form, so A cannot replace B or the reverse. B equals `static_cast<double>(raceDefOf(ctx, r).expFactor)`, so it is a projection of A's result. Both index `ctx.data.races` the same way with no bounds check.

what_a: Looks up a string value by key in the session's featureState map for the seer's pending person offer, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Records a pending "person" encounter offer from the seer in the feature state, storing the offered person's name and level so the offer can be answered later.
diff: Not comparable on any input. A reads `featureState[key]` and returns the value or an empty `Str`, leaving the session unchanged. B writes three keys (`kSeerKindKey`, `kSeerNameKey`, `kSeerLevelKey`) and returns nothing.

what_a: Handles the typed "quest <member>" command by checking that a named party member belongs to the Nomad guild, then assigning them a guild quest if none is open and replying with the appropriate message.
what_b: Handles the player's typed `titles <member>` command by looking up the named party member's Nomad guild membership and replying with their guild title and level, such as "Vagrant (1)", or an error message if the name is unknown or the member is not in a guild.
diff: Every input differs in outcome except the shared early exits. Both return the same usage error when `w.size() < 2` (different text: "Usage: quest <member>" vs "Usage: titles <member>"), and both return the same "No member called X." and "X is not in a guild." replies. Otherwise A assigns a guild quest and sets the open-quest flag, replying "You have also been assigned a Quest to complete." or "You still have your guild quest to complete." B only reads the guild title and level and replies "<Title> (<level>)" with no state change.

what_a: Rolls a percentage check by drawing a random number on the critical-chance scale and returning whether it falls below the given chance, which decides whether a player's critical hit or backstab proc triggers.
what_b: Rolls the player's critical-hit and backstab procs for a blow by calling a proc roll for each, with crit rolled first and backstab second, before the hit gate is applied.
diff: Not interchangeable for any input. A returns one bool from one RNG draw. B returns a BlowProcs struct with two flags (crit, backstab) and consumes two RNG draws, in that order, via two calls to A.

what_a: Returns the string value stored under a given key in the session's feature-state map, or an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Reads a numeric field from a JSON object by key, returning its value as a double or 0.0 if the key is absent.
diff: Not replaceable. A returns a `Str` (empty string when the key is absent) from `featureState`, while B returns a `double` (0.0 when absent or null) from a JSON object via `asDouble()`. They differ in return type, default value, container, and purpose, so no input makes them agree.

what_a: Returns the index of the first item in the item definition table whose type matches the given kind, or -1 if none does.
what_b: Returns the worn-class index for an item by looking up its type in the item-type table, returning 0 if the item has no definition or an invalid type; the file header notes the mapping is not a documented formula.
diff: Not replaceable at any call site. A scans `ctx.data.items` for the first entry whose `type` equals `kind` and returns its index or -1. B looks up one item's definition via `defOf(ctx, it.id)` and returns `ctx.data.itemTypes[type].index`, or 0 if the definition is missing or the type is out of range. They search different tables and return different quantities: a list position versus a field from the item-type table.

what_a: Handles the "seer person <name>" command by matching the typed name against party members, refusing if the character is in town or the name is unknown or ambiguous, and otherwise storing a pending search and replying with the depth-based fee and a yes-or-no prompt.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "seer" command, which lets the player search for a creature, item, or person for a fee, and answer yes or no to a pending offer.
diff: Every input differs. A takes (Session&, typed name, reply&) and returns bool, and it looks up a named character, validates the match, and sets a pending fee offer. B takes no arguments, returns void, and registers the "seer" command with the feature system, so no call site could swap one for the other.

what_a: Returns a read-only reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, converting the coordinates to a flat index via cellOf.
what_b: Returns a read-only reference to the party member at index i, converting the signed index to unsigned for the members array lookup without any game rule applied.
diff: The signatures differ: A takes (floor, x, y) and B takes (party, i), so call sites cannot be swapped without rewriting the arguments. A indexes `floor.squares` via `cellOf(x, y)` and returns a `SquareState`, while B indexes `p.members` directly by `i` and returns a `Character`. Negative inputs also convert differently: B's `static_cast<u32>` wraps a negative `i` to a large unsigned value, and A's result depends on `cellOf`, which is not shown.

what_a: Maps a single treasure-class roll against two box-chance thresholds, shifted by a bonus, to pick the chest treasure class (2 or 3, or none if neither threshold is met).
what_b: Returns the treasure-class bonus added to a chest roll, granting it only when the chest comes from a lair and the second box-chance value is positive.
diff: Not comparable as replacements. classFromThresholds returns a treasure class (kTreasureClassNone, 2, or 3) from a roll and two box thresholds, while lairBonusFor returns a bonus amount (kLairTreasureBonus or 0) from a lair flag and box2. They have different signatures, different return meanings, and different rules.

what_a: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string-valued key in a JSON object and returns its string value, or an empty string if the key is missing.
diff: (1) Key absent: A returns the caller's `dflt`, while B always returns an empty string, so they differ whenever `dflt` is non-empty. (2) Key present with a non-string JSON value (number, bool, null, object, array): A returns the stored `Str` unchanged, while B returns `v->asString()`, which may produce a different string or an empty one depending on how `asString` handles non-string types. (3) Argument forms differ (Session and Str key versus JsonValue and const char* key), which is permitted by the question.

what_a: Decrements the penned-companion count for a given reference and alignment in the pen book, bounded at zero and ignoring out-of-range indices.
what_b: Checks whether a given reference index and alignment index are in range and returns true only if the pen book holds at least one pen for that combination.
diff: releaseOne mutates the pen book by decrementing `byRef[ref][align]` (floored at 0) and returns void, while penTakeAllowed is a read-only predicate that returns true when the count is greater than 0 and never changes state. For every valid input, releaseOne changes the count and penTakeAllowed leaves it alone, so their results differ in kind and neither can replace the other.

what_a: Reads an integer field for a pending raise (resurrection) from the session's feature state by member and field name, returning the fallback value if the key is missing or the stored text doesn't parse as an integer.
what_b: Reads a boolean field by key from a JSON object, returning false if the key is missing.
diff: Not comparable as replacements. A returns an i32 looked up by member and field key from `s.featureState`, parsed with `rescueParseInt`, and falls back to a supplied default. B returns a bool read from a JSON object by key, with a fixed `false` default. Their input types, return types, and fallback semantics all differ, so no argument-form change would make one stand in for the other.

what_a: Builds the text shown for a spell-buffer slot in a party member's pack, showing the spell or item name and its cost, or "(Nothing)" when empty, and clears the slot's stored buffer when the item it refers to no longer exists.
what_b: Handles the player's typed `buffer` command, listing a party member's spell buffers or setting or clearing one of their four buffer slots to a named spell, and returning the reply text.
diff: Every input differs. buffersDescribe(s, member, slot) returns the display text for one slot (e.g. "\"Fireball\"  12", "(Nothing)", or "(unknown item)"), and it clears stale item and pack-slot buffers as a side effect. bufferCommand(s, words, reply) parses a player command, returns a usage, error, or confirmation message, and writes or erases the buffer. It never returns a description of a slot's contents.

what_a: Returns the item's alignment field as a 32-bit integer, with no game logic applied.
what_b: Returns the number of entries in the monsters table of the game data, as a 32-bit integer.
diff: Function A returns the item's alignment field cast to i32 and ignores everything else, so it takes an Item. Function B returns the number of entries in ctx.data.monsters cast to i32, so it takes a Ctx. For any inputs, the results are unrelated values (an alignment versus a monster count), and their argument types differ.

what_a: Copies named fields from a JSON object into a GuildDef struct, converting each value to an int, double, string, bool, or array as appropriate, with no game rules applied.
what_b: Copies the "areaId" and "flags" integer fields from a parsed JSON object into a FloorField struct, with no game rules applied.
diff: They read different types (GuildDef vs FloorField) and different keys. A reads 27 fields (tableIndex, name, maxLevel, ... hasSpellTable) and B reads only areaId and flags, so B cannot replace A at any call site, and A cannot replace B.

what_a: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
what_b: Converts a 32-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives and "0" for zero.
diff: Not interchangeable at any call site. parseNum takes a string and returns bool plus an i64 out-parameter (for example, "42" gives true and 42, "-" or "4x" gives false, and values above 1000000000000 give false). gearNum takes an i32 and returns a string (for example, 42 gives "42" and -2147483648 gives "-2147483648").

what_a: Searches a list of floor states for the one whose dungeon level matches the given level and returns its index, or -1 if none matches.
what_b: Scans the game's floor table for the entry whose level number matches the requested level and returns a pointer to it, or null if none exists.
diff: A searches `floors` (FloorState, field `dungeonLevel`) and returns the index of the first match as `i32`, or `-1` if none. B searches `data.floors` (FloorDef, field `levelNum`) and returns a pointer to the first match, or `nullptr` if none. Any call site must change its argument (vector vs. GameData) and its return handling (index/-1 vs. pointer/nullptr), and the two functions give different answers if the FloorState list and the static FloorDef list disagree about which levels exist.

what_a: Resolves one monster melee blow against the target, computing the damage the monster deals from its strength, level, and damage modifier (using a placeholder archive damage formula, since the real blow body isn't in the sources).
what_b: Computes the base melee damage a monster deals to a character each round, scaled by the monster's strength and guild level and reduced by the character's defence against the monster's attack, with a random roll.
diff: For every input where B's result fits in i32, A returns the same value and consumes the same RNG draws. A differs only when B's result exceeds INT32_MAX: A's `static_cast<i32>` then overflows (undefined behaviour in C++), while B returns the full value as f64. A's return type is also i32 rather than f64.

what_a: Totals the Att values of all equipped worn items, looking up each item's definition, to give the attack bonus contributed by the character's gear (the R2 attack-from-equipment rule).
what_b: Computes a character's attack rating (AttackOf) by summing the base attack value, the stat-derived attack bonus, the best guild attack bonus, and the equipped items' attack values, then clamping the result at zero.
diff: attackOf returns max(0, baseAD + statsAD + best guild AD + equippedAtt). equippedAtt returns only the raw sum of equipped Att. For example, with no equipped gear and nonzero baseAD, equippedAtt returns 0 while attackOf returns baseAD + statsAD + guild AD (clamped at 0). If the equipped sum is negative and the other terms are small, equippedAtt returns a negative value while attackOf returns 0.

what_a: Converts a 1-based item alignment value (Good, Neutral, Evil) into a 0-based pen index by subtracting one.
what_b: Maps a wearer's alignment (Good, Neutral, or Evil) to the alignment bit that item alignment restrictions are checked against, per game rule R11.
diff: For Good, Neutral, and Evil, A returns the pen index 0, 1, and 2, while B returns kAlignBitGood, kAlignBitNeutral, and kAlignBitEvil (the values of which aren't shown). B also returns 0 for an out-of-range Align value, while A returns static_cast<i32>(align) - 1 for any input. A's return type is i32 and B's is u32, and A takes ItemAlign while B takes Align.

what_a: Registers the town-screen "realign" command, which lets the player change an item's alignment for a fee, with its usage line shown to the player.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "seer" command, which lets the player search for a creature, item, or person for a fee, and answer yes or no to a pending offer.
diff: Every input differs. The command names are "realign" versus "seer", the handlers are cmdRealign versus seerCommand, and the usage strings describe unrelated actions (changing an item's alignment versus a Seer search).

what_a: Checks whether a buffer index falls within the range of pack slots, returning true only for valid item slot numbers.
what_b: Checks that an item's id is a positive number that falls within the range of the game's item table, so it can be safely used as an index into it.
diff: Every input where the two functions disagree. For example, b=0 gives true in A (when kPackSlots > 0) and false in B (since it requires id > 0). For b or id in [kPackSlots, items.size()), A returns false and B returns true. Negative values are rejected by both. A's upper bound is the compile-time constant kPackSlots, while B's is the runtime size of ctx.data.items. Their parameter types also differ (i32 buffer index vs. const Item&), so they cannot be substituted at call sites even with argument-form changes.

what_a: Resolves which guild membership a quest, claim, or titles command acts on, preferring the player's active guild if joined and otherwise the first joined guild, and returns null if the character is in none.
what_b: Checks whether a guild membership on a character is active (joined and at level above zero), and, for class-restricted items, whether that guild is the character's primary guild.
diff: They return different types and answer different questions. A returns a `GuildMembership*` (or nullptr) and writes the chosen guild to an out-parameter, while B returns a bool. A never checks `level`, so a joined guild at level 0 is still returned by A and rejected by B. A has no class-restriction parameter and always prefers the active guild, while B rejects any non-active guild only when `classRestricted` is true. A bounds-checks `activeGuild`, but B indexes `c.guilds[g]` without a check.

what_a: Returns a copy of the given string with every character converted to lowercase, which is used for case-insensitive INI key matching and has no game meaning.
what_b: Returns a copy of the input string with all ASCII uppercase letters converted to lowercase.
diff: Under the default "C" locale the two agree on every input. If the program calls setlocale() with a Latin-1-style locale, A also lowercases bytes 0xC0-0xDE (e.g. 0xC0 becomes 0xE0) while B leaves them unchanged, so the results differ for those non-ASCII bytes.

what_a: Records a pending "person" encounter offer from the seer in the feature state, storing the offered person's name and level so the offer can be answered later.
what_b: Registers the town-screen "seer" command, which lets the player search for a creature, item, or person for a fee, and answer yes or no to a pending offer.
diff: Not comparable on any input. A is a state setter that writes "person", the name, and the level into `s.featureState`. B takes no arguments and registers the "seer" command for the Town screen. They don't return values, mutate state, or serve the same role, so they can't replace each other at any call site.

what_a: Converts a 32-bit signed integer to its decimal string form, with a leading minus sign for negatives and "0" for zero.
what_b: Casts a signed 32-bit index to an unsigned 32-bit integer with no game meaning.
diff: Return types differ (Str vs. u32), so no call site can swap one for the other. For example, gearNum(42) returns "42" while uidx(42) returns 42u; gearNum(-1) returns "-1" while uidx(-1) returns 4294967295u.

what_a: Registers four town-screen player commands (quest, claim, forfeit, titles) that let a member show or assign a guild quest, claim a completed quest or guildmastership, leave a guild, or show their guild title.
what_b: Rolls a quest for a guild member at the given guild level, returning none, a let-off, a defeat quest, or a fetch quest based on the SRD's quest percentages and level thresholds.
diff: Function A returns nothing and registers four Town-screen commands (quest, claim, forfeit, titles) with their handlers and help text. Function B takes a context, membership, guild definition, and guild level and returns a quest outcome (kRollNone, kRollLetOff, kRollDefeat, or kRollFetch) after drawing random numbers. They have different signatures, return types, and side effects, so no input produces matching results.

what_a: Returns the trap chance for a chest's treasure class (0 to 3), giving 0 for any out-of-range class, as set by the game's chest trap table.
what_b: Repeatedly draws random trap-bit indices (up to a capped number of attempts) and returns the first index whose bit is set in the chest's trap flags, or -1 if none is found, which selects which trap a chest triggers.
diff: Not comparable. A maps a treasure class (0-3, otherwise 0) to a trap chance from a table. B takes a bitmask, randomly draws bit indices up to kTrapDrawAttempts times, and returns the first set bit's index or -1. For example, A(2) returns kTrapChanceByClass[2], while B with trapFlags=0 always returns -1 and A(5) returns 0.

what_a: Formats a 64-bit integer as a decimal string, with no game meaning.
what_b: Rounds a double to four decimal places using half-even rounding and returns it as a 64-bit fixed-point integer, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: Function A takes an integer and returns its decimal text (e.g. `numText(42)` returns `"42"`). Function B takes a double and returns an integer scaled by 10000 with half-even rounding (e.g. `curFixed(1.23456)` returns `12346`). Their return types differ (string vs. i64), so neither can replace the other at a call site.

what_a: Copies the fields of a JSON object into a RaceDef struct by key name (numbers, strings, and arrays), with no game rules applied.
what_b: Copies named fields from a JSON object into a GuildDef struct, converting each value to an int, double, string, bool, or array as appropriate, with no game rules applied.
diff: Function A reads the fields tableIndex, name, min, max, size, alignMask, bonusPoints, maxAge, expFactor, resistances, alignments, minTotal, maxTotal; Function B reads tableIndex, name, maxLevel, reqStats, alignMask, raceMask, avgHits, hitsCapLevel, lateHits, attPerLevel, defPerLevel, goldFactor, itemUseFactor, adMaxLevel, adEvery, abilities, thieving, backstab, criticalHit, extraSwings, perception, expFactor, questPercent, spellRate, spellMax, hasSpellTable. They populate different structs (RaceDef vs GuildDef) with mostly different fields, so they cannot be substituted for one another at any call site.

what_a: Checks whether a given square on a dungeon floor (1-based x, y coordinates) has a specific flag set, returning false for out-of-bounds coordinates.
what_b: Returns a pointer to the square at 1-based coordinates (x, y) in a floor's row-major square array, or nullptr if the coordinates fall outside the 30-wide map or past the end of the stored squares.
diff: Different return types: A returns a bool (whether the flag bit is set), B returns a `const SquareState*` (or nullptr), so they can't substitute for each other at any call site. A also takes its row width from `def.width` and rejects `width <= 0`, while B uses the fixed `kViewMapWidth`, so for any floor whose width differs from `kViewMapWidth` they map (x, y) to different indices. A also tests a `FloorFlag` bit, which B has no equivalent for.

what_a: Looks up an item definition by its numeric id, returning a pointer into the item table or null when the id is zero, negative, or out of range.
what_b: Linear search through the game's item list that returns a pointer to the item definition whose id matches the given id, or null if none exists.
diff: They agree only when `items[k].id == k` for every element and no element has id 0. Otherwise they differ: (1) an id of 0 or below returns nullptr from A, but B returns the element whose id is 0 if one exists; (2) an id at or beyond `items.size()` returns nullptr from A, but B returns the element if some `d.id` equals it; (3) if `items[k].id != k` for some k, A returns `items[id]` while B returns the element whose `id` field matches, so they return different items; (4) with duplicate ids, B returns the first match in array order, while A returns the element at index `id`.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Formats a 64-bit integer as a decimal string, with no game meaning.
diff: They are inverse operations with different signatures. glParseInt takes a string and returns an integer, setting ok to false for empty input, a lone "-", "+5", leading or trailing whitespace, or any other non-digit. numText takes an integer and returns its decimal string, with no failure case. No call site could swap one for the other, even with argument changes.

what_a: Converts a buffer index into a spell index by subtracting the pack slot count, a pure index conversion with no game meaning of its own.
what_b: Converts a 0-based pack index into a 1-based player slot number by adding one, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: A computes b - kPackSlots and B computes packIndex + 1, so they agree only when kPackSlots = -1 (for example, b = 0 gives -kPackSlots for A and 1 for B, which match only when kPackSlots = -1). The value of kPackSlots isn't in the snippet, so I can't rule out that exact case, but for any other value they differ for every input.

what_a: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
what_b: Parses a string as a signed 64-bit decimal integer, rejecting any non-digit characters or overflow, and writes the result to the output parameter.
diff: Both reject empty strings, "+5", "-" alone, and any non-digit characters, and both leave `out` untouched on failure. They differ on: "-5" and other negative values (A rejects, B accepts); "1000001" through "9223372036854775807" (A rejects because it caps at 1000000, B accepts); "-9223372036854775808" (B rejects, since its accumulator can't reach 2^63); and the output type (A writes i32, B writes i64, so B can return values that A can't represent).

what_a: Scans the game data's item list for the entry whose id matches the given id and returns a pointer to it, or null if none matches.
what_b: Returns the index of the first item in the item definition table whose type matches the given kind, or -1 if none does.
diff: Function A matches `data.items[i].id == id` and returns a pointer to the item or `nullptr`; Function B matches `static_cast<i32>(items[i].type) == kind` and returns the index or `-1`. They differ on every input where the key and the match semantics disagree: an id lookup and a type lookup with the same numeric value can return different items, and A's not-found result is a null pointer where B's is `-1`.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 6 decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, returning false if any character is not a digit or the string is empty or too long.
what_b: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
diff: A rejects any string with a leading '-' (e.g. "-5" gives false), while B accepts it (ok=true, returns -5). A rejects strings longer than 6 characters (e.g. "1234567" or "0000001" gives false), while B accepts them (1234567 and 1, respectively). For 19+ digit inputs B overflows i64 (undefined behaviour), whereas A's length cap prevents this. Both reject "", "-", "+5", and "12a", and both accept "000001" as 1.

what_a: Looks up the square at the given x, y coordinates on a dungeon floor, using the floor's width from the game data (or a default width), and returns a pointer to it or null if the level or coordinates are invalid.
what_b: Converts 1-based (x, y) grid coordinates into an index in the flat square array of a floor, returning a pointer to that square or nullptr if the coordinates or index fall outside the map.
diff: (1) Level < 1: A returns nullptr; B has no level argument. (2) Width: A uses the floor's width from `s.data.floors`, or `kRescueDefaultWidth` if no definition exists; B always uses `kMapWidth`. They differ whenever those widths differ. (3) x > width: A doesn't check this, so x = width+1 wraps to x = 1 of the next row; B returns nullptr for x > kMapWidth. (4) x < 1: A wraps to the previous row when y ≥ 2 (e.g. x=0, y=2 returns the square at (width, 1)); B returns nullptr. (5) y < 1: A can return a square when x > width (e.g. x=width+1, y=0 returns (1,1)); B returns nullptr. (6) A returns nullptr when no floor matches `level`, which B has no equivalent for.

what_a: Computes a character's total attack and defence values by combining guild-based A/D, stat-derived A/D, worn-item A/D, and the stored A/D shift, as the game's R13 rule defines.
what_b: Computes a character's combat armour/defence rating (the attack-side AD figure) as a base value plus stat-derived, stored-shift, best guild award and fitted worn-item bonuses, clamped at zero.
diff: (1) B clamps its result at 0 and A does not, so any input where the attack total is negative (for example, statAD + shift + guild + item below zero) gives A a negative value and B 0. (2) B adds the constant kBaseAD and A does not, so they differ for every input unless kBaseAD = 0. (3) B uses raw best.att, while A uses guildAD(bestGuildPair(c)).att, so they differ whenever guildAD changes the guild award. (4) B returns one attack-side number, while A returns the (att, def) pair, so B has no defence result to compare with A's def.

what_a: Computes a player's melee damage against a defence of 0 by folding guild level, fighting and weapon modifiers, critical hit, backstab, unseen status and size difference into a damage modifier, then resolves the hit and damage using strength.
what_b: Resolves one monster melee blow against the target, computing the damage the monster deals from its strength, level, and damage modifier (using a placeholder archive damage formula, since the real blow body isn't in the sources).
diff: Function A applies the R16/R21/R23 player melee path (characterDamageMod, then meleeHitAndDamage with defence 0, guildLevel, strength), while Function B is a placeholder that calls archiveMonsterDamage with monster strength/level and no guild or player modifiers, and it omits the R35 LN(DamMod)^2 reduction; their results differ for essentially all inputs, and B's own comment marks its body as unknown and in conflict with the engine form.

what_a: Returns the spell point cost to cast a spell, which is zero when the cast comes from an item (itemLevel nonzero) and otherwise is the caster's spellbook cost from the spell cost engine.
what_b: Handles the player's typed "cast <member> <spell>" command in the dungeon, checking the caster and spell, applying the gate, reach and spell-point rules, and returning a message for the player.
diff: Function A returns an i32 SP cost (0 when itemLevel != 0, otherwise spellCostEngine's result) and has no side effects. Function B is a command handler that takes a session and word list, returns bool, writes a reply string, checks gates and reach, and deducts SP from the caster after applying the effect. It calls castCostSp internally with itemLevel 0, so they are not interchangeable at any call site.

what_a: Tests whether a given bit (0–31) is set in a 32-bit flags value, returning false for out-of-range bit indices.
what_b: Reinterprets a signed 32-bit integer as an unsigned 32-bit integer for indexing, with no game meaning.
diff: A takes (u32 flags, i32 bit) and returns bool; B takes (i32 i) and returns u32. A tests a bit and returns true/false, while B reinterprets a signed int as unsigned. No input gives the same result from both, so neither can replace the other, even with argument changes.

what_a: Reads one stored Hall of Records value (a stat or achievement record, keyed by record index and field name) from session feature state and parses it into a 64-bit integer.
what_b: Looks up a stored record field (for a given kind and name, such as a monster or item entry) in the session's feature state and returns its string value, or an empty string if it is absent.
diff: Different return types: A returns `i64` (a parsed integer) and B returns `Str` (the raw stored string). Different lookup keys: A is indexed by `k` through `hallGetS`, while B builds the key `kRecordPrefix + kind + "." + name + "." + field` from a kind and a name. B returns an empty string for a missing key, but A's behaviour for a missing or non-numeric value depends on `hallGetS` and `hallParseI`, which are not shown. A parses its value and B does not.

what_a: Handles the "hall" command by building a text reply that lists the header "Hall of Records" followed by a description of each of the twelve records.
what_b: Handles the player's roster command by building a reply that describes the current party and then lists each character not in the party.
diff: Not applicable. A builds "Hall of Records" followed by hallDescribe(s, k) for each hall index k, while B sets reply to describeParty(s) and appends "Not in party: <name>" for each name in rosterLeftBehind(s). Their outputs differ for every input.

what_a: Linearly searches the left-behind list for an entry whose name matches the given name and returns its index, or -1 if none matches.
what_b: Returns the index of the item definition in the data table whose id matches the given item's id, or -1 if none is found.
diff: They search different collections with different predicates and argument types. A takes a `Vec<Str>` of names and a `Str` name, and matches with `sameName`. B takes a `Ctx` and an `Item`, and matches `Item.id` against `ItemDef.id` in `ctx.data.items`. No input can make them agree at a call site, since the argument types and the matched fields differ.

what_a: Formats a gold amount stored in 1/10000 gold units as a decimal string with a " gold" suffix, omitting the fractional part when it is zero.
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold amount as a human-readable string with up to four decimal places and trailing zeros removed, followed by " gold".
diff: (1) Trailing zeros in the fraction: A always prints four fraction digits, B drops trailing zeros. For units=5000, A gives "0.5000 gold" and B gives "0.5 gold". For units=10001 both give "1.0001 gold". (2) Negative units: A has no sign handling. For units=-5000 it gives whole=0 and emits non-digit characters from the negative remainder (e.g. '+'); for units=-15000 it gives a malformed string. B gives "-0.5 gold" and "-1.5 gold". Non-negative inputs with zero fraction (e.g. 10000 → "1 gold") and non-negative inputs with fractions that have no trailing zeros (e.g. 10001) match.

what_a: Counts how many entries on the store shelf have a given alignment, returning the tally as an integer.
what_b: Counts how many monsters in the encounter still have hit points above zero, so the combat logic can tell how many foes are left standing.
diff: They take different input types (`Vec<Item>` plus an `ItemAlign` argument versus an `Encounter`), test different predicates (`it.alignment == align` versus `monsters[i].hits > 0`), and serve different purposes (R16 store shelf counting versus living-foe counting in combat), so no input makes them interchangeable.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
what_b: Parses a string as a signed 64-bit decimal integer, rejecting any non-digit characters or overflow, and writes the result to the output parameter.
diff: (1) Leading '-': B accepts "-5" (out = -5) and "-0" (out = 0); A returns false for both. (2) Length: A returns false for any input longer than 4 characters, so "00001" and "10000" are rejected; B accepts them ("00001" gives 1, "10000" gives 10000). (3) Range: A caps at 9999; B accepts up to kI64Max (and down to -kI64Max). (4) Output type: A writes an i32, B an i64, so call sites must change their variable type as well as their argument form.
